Use: APT28 has used CVE-2015-1701 to access the SYSTEM token and copy it into the current process as part of privilege escalation. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2015/04/probable_apt28_useo.html

APT28 has used a Powershell cmdlet to grant the ApplicationImpersonation role to a compromised account. https://media.defense.gov/2021/Jul/01/2002753896/-1/-1/1/CSA_GRU_GLOBAL_BRUTE_FORCE_CAMPAIGN_UOO158036-21.PDF

APT28 registered domains imitating NATO, OSCE security websites, Caucasus information resources, and other organizations.   https://www.fireeye.com/content/dam/fireeye-www/global/en/current-threats/pdfs/rpt-apt28.pdf
APT28 has used newly-created Blogspot pages for credential harvesting operations. https://blog.google/threat-analysis-group/update-threat-landscape-ukraine
APT28 has performed large-scale scans in an attempt to find vulnerable servers. https://documents.trendmicro.com/assets/white_papers/wp-pawn-storm-in-2019.pdf

Later implants used by APT28, such as CHOPSTICK, use a blend of HTTP, HTTPS, and other legitimate channels for C2, depending on module configuration.  https://www.fireeye.com/content/dam/fireeye-www/global/en/current-threats/pdfs/rpt-apt28.pdf

APT28 has used IMAP, POP3, and SMTP for a communication channel in various implants, including using self-registered Google Mail accounts and later compromised email servers of its victims.  https://www.fireeye.com/content/dam/fireeye-www/global/en/current-threats/pdfs/rpt-apt28.pdf
APT28 used a publicly available tool to gather and compress multiple documents on the DCCC and DNC networks. https://www.justice.gov/file/1080281/download

APT28 has used a variety of utilities, including WinRAR, to archive collected data with password protection. https://media.defense.gov/2021/Jul/01/2002753896/-1/-1/1/CSA_GRU_GLOBAL_BRUTE_FORCE_CAMPAIGN_UOO158036-21.PDF
APT28 used a publicly available tool to gather and compress multiple documents on the DCCC and DNC networks. https://www.justice.gov/file/1080281/download
APT28 has deployed malware that has copied itself to the startup directory for persistence. https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/20/l/pawn-storm-lack-of-sophistication-as-a-strategy.html
An APT28 loader Trojan adds the Registry key HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript to establish persistence. https://pan-unit42.github.io/playbook_viewer/
APT28 can perform brute force attacks to obtain credentials.   https://documents.trendmicro.com/assets/white_papers/wp-pawn-storm-in-2019.pdf

APT28 has used a brute-force/password-spray tooling that operated in two modes: in brute-force mode it typically sent over 300 authentication attempts per hour per targeted account over the course of several hours or days.  APT28 has also used a Kubernetes cluster to conduct distributed, large-scale password guessing attacks. https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2020/09/10/strontium-detecting-new-patters-credential-harvesting/

APT28 has used a brute-force/password-spray tooling that operated in two modes: in password-spraying mode it conducted approximately four authentication attempts per hour per targeted account over the course of several days or weeks.   APT28 has also used a Kubernetes cluster to conduct distributed, large-scale password spray attacks. https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2020/09/10/strontium-detecting-new-patters-credential-harvesting/
APT28 downloads and executes PowerShell scripts and performs PowerShell commands.   https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2018/06/unit42-sofacy-groups-parallel-attacks/
An APT28 loader Trojan uses a cmd.exe and batch script to run its payload.  The group has also used macros to execute payloads.    https://pan-unit42.github.io/playbook_viewer/

APT28 uses a tool that captures information from air-gapped computers via an infected USB and transfers it to network-connected computer when the USB is inserted. http://download.microsoft.com/download/4/4/C/44CDEF0E-7924-4787-A56A-16261691ACE3/Microsoft_Security_Intelligence_Report_Volume_19_English.pdf
APT28 has used compromised email accounts to send credential phishing emails. https://blog.google/threat-analysis-group/update-threat-landscape-ukraine
APT28 has collected files from various information repositories. https://media.defense.gov/2021/Jul/01/2002753896/-1/-1/1/CSA_GRU_GLOBAL_BRUTE_FORCE_CAMPAIGN_UOO158036-21.PDF

APT28 has collected information from Microsoft SharePoint services within target networks. https://paper.seebug.org/papers/APT/APT_CyberCriminal_Campagin/2015/2015.11.04_Evolving_Threats/cct-w08_evolving-threats-dissection-of-a-cyber-espionage-attack.pdf

APT28 has retrieved internal documents from machines inside victim environments, including by using Forfiles to stage documents before exfiltration.    https://netzpolitik.org/2015/digital-attack-on-german-parliament-investigative-report-on-the-hack-of-the-left-party-infrastructure-in-bundestag/
APT28 has collected files from network shared drives. https://media.defense.gov/2021/Jul/01/2002753896/-1/-1/1/CSA_GRU_GLOBAL_BRUTE_FORCE_CAMPAIGN_UOO158036-21.PDF

An APT28 backdoor may collect the entire contents of an inserted USB device. http://download.microsoft.com/download/4/4/C/44CDEF0E-7924-4787-A56A-16261691ACE3/Microsoft_Security_Intelligence_Report_Volume_19_English.pdf

APT28 added "junk data" to each encoded string, preventing trivial decoding without knowledge of the junk removal algorithm. Each implant was given a "junk length" value when created, tracked by the controller software to allow seamless communication but prevent analysis of the command protocol on the wire. https://www.fireeye.com/content/dam/fireeye-www/global/en/current-threats/pdfs/rpt-apt28.pdf

APT28 has stored captured credential information in a file named pi.log. http://download.microsoft.com/download/4/4/C/44CDEF0E-7924-4787-A56A-16261691ACE3/Microsoft_Security_Intelligence_Report_Volume_19_English.pdf

APT28 has staged archives of collected data on a target's Outlook Web Access (OWA) server. https://media.defense.gov/2021/Jul/01/2002753896/-1/-1/1/CSA_GRU_GLOBAL_BRUTE_FORCE_CAMPAIGN_UOO158036-21.PDF
APT28 has split archived exfiltration files into chunks smaller than 1MB. https://media.defense.gov/2021/Jul/01/2002753896/-1/-1/1/CSA_GRU_GLOBAL_BRUTE_FORCE_CAMPAIGN_UOO158036-21.PDF

An APT28 macro uses the command certutil -decode to decode contents of a .txt file storing the base64 encoded payload.  https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2018/02/unit42-sofacy-attacks-multiple-government-entities/
APT28 has compromised targets via strategic web compromise utilizing custom exploit kits. https://www.secureworks.com/research/iron-twilight-supports-active-measures
APT28 has collected emails from victim Microsoft Exchange servers.  https://www.justice.gov/file/1080281/download
APT28 installed a Delphi backdoor that used a custom algorithm for C2 communications. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2019/05/22/journey-zebrocy-land/
APT28 has used COM hijacking for persistence by replacing the legitimate MMDeviceEnumerator object with a payload.  http://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/eset-sednit-part1.pdf

APT28 has exfiltrated archives of collected data previously staged on a target's OWA server via HTTPS. https://media.defense.gov/2021/Jul/01/2002753896/-1/-1/1/CSA_GRU_GLOBAL_BRUTE_FORCE_CAMPAIGN_UOO158036-21.PDF
APT28 can exfiltrate data over Google Drive. https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/20/l/pawn-storm-lack-of-sophistication-as-a-strategy.html

APT28 has used a variety of public exploits, including CVE 2020-0688 and CVE 2020-17144, to gain execution on vulnerable Microsoft Exchange; they have also conducted SQL injection attacks against external websites.  https://www.justice.gov/opa/page/file/1098481/download
APT28 has exploited Microsoft Office vulnerability CVE-2017-0262 for execution. https://securelist.com/a-slice-of-2017-sofacy-activity/83930/

APT28 has used CVE-2015-4902 to bypass security features.  https://download.bitdefender.com/resources/media/materials/white-papers/en/Bitdefender_In-depth_analysis_of_APT28%E2%80%93The_Political_Cyber-Espionage.pdf

APT28 has exploited CVE-2014-4076, CVE-2015-2387, CVE-2015-1701, CVE-2017-0263 to escalate privileges.   https://download.bitdefender.com/resources/media/materials/white-papers/en/Bitdefender_In-depth_analysis_of_APT28%E2%80%93The_Political_Cyber-Espionage.pdf
APT28 exploited a Windows SMB Remote Code Execution Vulnerability to conduct lateral movement.   https://www.fireeye.com/content/dam/fireeye-www/global/en/current-threats/pdfs/rpt-apt28.pdf

APT28 has used Tor and a variety of commercial VPN services to route brute force authentication attempts. https://media.defense.gov/2021/Jul/01/2002753896/-1/-1/1/CSA_GRU_GLOBAL_BRUTE_FORCE_CAMPAIGN_UOO158036-21.PDF

APT28 has used Forfiles to locate PDF, Excel, and Word documents during collection. The group also searched a compromised DCCC computer for specific terms.  https://netzpolitik.org/2015/digital-attack-on-german-parliament-investigative-report-on-the-hack-of-the-left-party-infrastructure-in-bundestag/
APT28 has harvested user's login credentials. https://blogs.microsoft.com/on-the-issues/2020/09/10/cyberattacks-us-elections-trump-biden/
APT28 has saved files with hidden file attributes.  https://blog.talosintelligence.com/2017/10/cyber-conflict-decoy-document.html
APT28 has used the WindowStyle parameter to conceal PowerShell windows.   https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2018/06/unit42-sofacy-groups-parallel-attacks/
APT28 has cleared event logs, including by using the commands wevtutil cl System and wevtutil cl Security.  https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/
APT28 has intentionally deleted computer files to cover their tracks, including with use of the program CCleaner. https://www.justice.gov/file/1080281/download
APT28 has performed timestomping on victim files. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/

APT28 has downloaded additional files, including by using a first-stage downloader to contact the C2 server to obtain the second-stage implant.     https://download.bitdefender.com/resources/media/materials/white-papers/en/Bitdefender_In-depth_analysis_of_APT28%E2%80%93The_Political_Cyber-Espionage.pdf
APT28 has used tools to perform keylogging.   http://download.microsoft.com/download/4/4/C/44CDEF0E-7924-4787-A56A-16261691ACE3/Microsoft_Security_Intelligence_Report_Volume_19_English.pdf

APT28 has delivered JHUHUGIT and Koadic by executing PowerShell commands through DDE in Word documents.   https://securingtomorrow.mcafee.com/mcafee-labs/apt28-threat-group-adopts-dde-technique-nyc-attack-theme-in-latest-campaign/
APT28 has renamed the WinRAR utility to avoid detection. https://media.defense.gov/2021/Jul/01/2002753896/-1/-1/1/CSA_GRU_GLOBAL_BRUTE_FORCE_CAMPAIGN_UOO158036-21.PDF

APT28 has changed extensions on files containing exfiltrated data to make them appear benign, and renamed a web shell instance to appear as a legitimate OWA page. https://media.defense.gov/2021/Jul/01/2002753896/-1/-1/1/CSA_GRU_GLOBAL_BRUTE_FORCE_CAMPAIGN_UOO158036-21.PDF
In 2016, APT28 conducted a distributed denial of service (DDoS) attack against the World Anti-Doping Agency. https://www.justice.gov/opa/page/file/1098481/download

APT28 deployed the open source tool Responder to conduct NetBIOS Name Service poisoning, which captured usernames and hashed passwords that allowed access to legitimate credentials.   APT28 close-access teams have used Wi-Fi pineapples to intercept Wi-Fi signals and user credentials. https://www.fireeye.com/content/dam/fireeye-www/global/en/current-threats/pdfs/rpt-apt28.pdf

APT28 encrypted a .dll payload using RTL and a custom encryption algorithm. APT28 has also obfuscated payloads with base64, XOR, and RC4.     https://download.bitdefender.com/resources/media/materials/white-papers/en/Bitdefender_In-depth_analysis_of_APT28%E2%80%93The_Political_Cyber-Espionage.pdf
APT28 has obtained and used open-source tools like Koadic, Mimikatz, and Responder.   https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2018/06/unit42-sofacy-groups-parallel-attacks/

APT28 has used the Office Test persistence mechanism within Microsoft Office by adding the Registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Office test\Special\Perf to execute code. https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2016/07/unit42-technical-walkthrough-office-test-persistence-method-used-in-recent-sofacy-attacks/
APT28 regularly deploys both publicly available (ex: Mimikatz) and custom password retrieval tools on victims.   http://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/eset-sednit-part-2.pdf

APT28 regularly deploys both publicly available (ex: Mimikatz) and custom password retrieval tools on victims.   They have also dumped the LSASS process memory using the MiniDump function. http://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/eset-sednit-part-2.pdf

APT28 has used the ntdsutil.exe utility to export the Active Directory database for credential access. https://media.defense.gov/2021/Jul/01/2002753896/-1/-1/1/CSA_GRU_GLOBAL_BRUTE_FORCE_CAMPAIGN_UOO158036-21.PDF

APT28 uses a module to receive a notification every time a USB mass storage device is inserted into a victim. http://download.microsoft.com/download/4/4/C/44CDEF0E-7924-4787-A56A-16261691ACE3/Microsoft_Security_Intelligence_Report_Volume_19_English.pdf

APT28 sent spearphishing emails containing malicious Microsoft Office and RAR attachments.        https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2018/02/unit42-sofacy-attacks-multiple-government-entities/

APT28 sent spearphishing emails which used a URL-shortener service to masquerade as a legitimate service and to redirect targets to credential harvesting sites.    https://www.justice.gov/file/1080281/download
APT28 has used spearphishing to compromise credentials.  https://blogs.microsoft.com/on-the-issues/2020/09/10/cyberattacks-us-elections-trump-biden/
APT28 has conducted credential phishing campaigns with embedded links to attacker-controlled domains. https://blog.google/threat-analysis-group/update-threat-landscape-ukraine

APT28 has deployed a bootkit along with Downdelph to ensure its persistence on the victim. The bootkit shares code with some variants of BlackEnergy. http://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/eset-sednit-part3.pdf
An APT28 loader Trojan will enumerate the victim's processes searching for explorer.exe if its current process does not have necessary permissions. https://pan-unit42.github.io/playbook_viewer/

APT28 used other victims as proxies to relay command traffic, for instance using a compromised Georgian military email server as a hop point to NATO victims. The group has also used a tool that acts as a proxy to allow C2 even if the victim is behind a router. APT28 has also used a machine to relay and obscure communications between CHOPSTICK and their server.   https://www.fireeye.com/content/dam/fireeye-www/global/en/current-threats/pdfs/rpt-apt28.pdf
APT28 has routed traffic over Tor and VPN servers to obfuscate their activities. https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/20/l/pawn-storm-lack-of-sophistication-as-a-strategy.html
APT28 has mapped network drives using Net and administrator credentials. https://media.defense.gov/2021/Jul/01/2002753896/-1/-1/1/CSA_GRU_GLOBAL_BRUTE_FORCE_CAMPAIGN_UOO158036-21.PDF

APT28 uses a tool to infect connected USB devices and transmit itself to air-gapped computers when the infected USB device is inserted. http://download.microsoft.com/download/4/4/C/44CDEF0E-7924-4787-A56A-16261691ACE3/Microsoft_Security_Intelligence_Report_Volume_19_English.pdf
APT28 has used a UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface) rootkit known as LoJax.  https://www.symantec.com/blogs/election-security/apt28-espionage-military-government
APT28 has used tools to take screenshots from victims.    http://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/eset-sednit-part-2.pdf

APT28 has used a modified and obfuscated version of the reGeorg web shell to maintain persistence on a target's Outlook Web Access (OWA) server. https://media.defense.gov/2021/Jul/01/2002753896/-1/-1/1/CSA_GRU_GLOBAL_BRUTE_FORCE_CAMPAIGN_UOO158036-21.PDF

APT28 has used several malicious applications to steal user OAuth access tokens including applications masquerading as "Google Defender" "Google Email Protection," and "Google Scanner" for Gmail users. They also targeted Yahoo users with applications masquerading as "Delivery Service" and "McAfee Email Protection". https://blog.trendmicro.com/trendlabs-security-intelligence/pawn-storm-abuses-open-authentication-advanced-social-engineering-attacks

APT28 executed CHOPSTICK by using rundll32 commands such as rundll32.exe "C:\Windows\twain_64.dll". APT28 also executed a .dll for a first stage dropper using rundll32.exe. An APT28 loader Trojan saved a batch script that uses rundll32 to execute a DLL payload.      https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/
APT28 used weaponized Microsoft Word documents abusing the remote template function to retrieve a malicious macro.  https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/dear-joohn-sofacy-groups-global-campaign/
Once APT28 gained access to the DCCC network, the group then proceeded to use that access to compromise the DNC network. https://www.justice.gov/file/1080281/download

APT28 has used several malicious applications that abused OAuth access tokens to gain access to target email accounts, including Gmail and Yahoo Mail. https://blog.trendmicro.com/trendlabs-security-intelligence/pawn-storm-abuses-open-authentication-advanced-social-engineering-attacks
APT28 has used pass the hash for lateral movement. http://download.microsoft.com/download/4/4/C/44CDEF0E-7924-4787-A56A-16261691ACE3/Microsoft_Security_Intelligence_Report_Volume_19_English.pdf
APT28 has tricked unwitting recipients into clicking on malicious hyperlinks within emails crafted to resemble trustworthy senders.  https://www.justice.gov/opa/page/file/1098481/download

APT28 attempted to get users to click on Microsoft Office attachments containing malicious macro scripts.   https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2018/02/unit42-sofacy-attacks-multiple-government-entities/

APT28 has used legitimate credentials to gain initial access, maintain access, and exfiltrate data from a victim network. The group has specifically used credentials stolen through a spearphishing email to login to the DCCC network. The group has also leveraged default manufacturer's passwords to gain initial access to corporate networks via IoT devices such as a VOIP phone, printer, and video decoder.    https://documents.trendmicro.com/assets/wp/wp-two-years-of-pawn-storm.pdf

APT28 has used compromised Office 365 service accounts with Global Administrator privileges to collect email from user inboxes. https://media.defense.gov/2021/Jul/01/2002753896/-1/-1/1/CSA_GRU_GLOBAL_BRUTE_FORCE_CAMPAIGN_UOO158036-21.PDF
APT28 has used Google Drive for C2. https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/20/l/pawn-storm-lack-of-sophistication-as-a-strategy.html

Use: APT29 has bypassed UAC. http://www.slideshare.net/MatthewDunwoody1/no-easy-breach-derby-con-2016

APT29 obtained a list of users and their roles from an Exchange server using Get-ManagementRoleAssignment. https://www.volexity.com/blog/2020/12/14/dark-halo-leverages-solarwinds-compromise-to-breach-organizations/
APT29 has used PowerShell to discover domain accounts by executing Get-ADUser and Get-ADGroupMember.  https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/observations-from-the-stellarparticle-campaign/
APT29 has conducted enumeration of Azure AD accounts. https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2021/10/25/nobelium-targeting-delegated-administrative-privileges-to-facilitate-broader-attacks/
APT29 has added credentials to OAuth Applications and Service Principals.  https://msrc-blog.microsoft.com/2020/12/13/customer-guidance-on-recent-nation-state-cyber-attacks/

APT29 added their own devices as allowed IDs for active sync using Set-CASMailbox, allowing it to obtain copies of victim mailboxes. It also added additional permissions (such as Mail.Read and Mail.ReadWrite) to compromised Application or Service Principals.   https://www.volexity.com/blog/2020/12/14/dark-halo-leverages-solarwinds-compromise-to-breach-organizations/
APT29 has granted company administrator privileges to a newly created service principal. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/observations-from-the-stellarparticle-campaign/
APT29 registered devices in order to enable mailbox syncing via the Set-CASMailbox command. https://www.volexity.com/blog/2020/12/14/dark-halo-leverages-solarwinds-compromise-to-breach-organizations/
APT29 has acquired C2 domains, sometimes through resellers.   https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2021/03/04/goldmax-goldfinder-sibot-analyzing-nobelium-malware/

APT29 has registered algorithmically generated Twitter handles that are used for C2 by malware, such as HAMMERTOSS. APT29 has also used legitimate web services such as Dropbox and Constant Contact in their operations.  https://www2.fireeye.com/rs/848-DID-242/images/rpt-apt29-hammertoss.pdf
APT29 has conducted widespread scanning of target environments to identify vulnerabilities for exploit. https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/files/Advisory-further-TTPs-associated-with-SVR-cyber-actors.pdf
APT29 has used HTTP for C2 and data exfiltration. https://www.volexity.com/blog/2020/12/14/dark-halo-leverages-solarwinds-compromise-to-breach-organizations/

APT29 used 7-Zip to compress stolen emails into password-protected archives prior to exfiltration; APT29 has also compressed text files into zipped archives.   https://www.volexity.com/blog/2020/12/14/dark-halo-leverages-solarwinds-compromise-to-breach-organizations/
APT29 added Registry Run keys to establish persistence. http://www.slideshare.net/MatthewDunwoody1/no-easy-breach-derby-con-2016
APT29 has conducted brute force password spray attacks.  https://msrc-blog.microsoft.com/2021/06/25/new-nobelium-activity/

APT29 has used encoded PowerShell scripts uploaded to CozyCar installations to download and install SeaDuke. APT29 also used PowerShell to create new tasks on remote machines, identify configuration settings, evade defenses, exfiltrate data, and to execute other commands.        https://www.volexity.com/blog/2020/12/14/dark-halo-leverages-solarwinds-compromise-to-breach-organizations/
APT29 used cmd.exe to execute commands on remote machines.  https://www.volexity.com/blog/2020/12/14/dark-halo-leverages-solarwinds-compromise-to-breach-organizations/
APT29 has written malware variants in Visual Basic. https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/files/Advisory-further-TTPs-associated-with-SVR-cyber-actors.pdf
APT29 has developed malware variants written in Python. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/ESET_Operation_Ghost_Dukes.pdf
APT29 has compromised email accounts to further enable phishing campaigns. https://www.cert.ssi.gouv.fr/uploads/CERTFR-2021-CTI-011.pdf
APT29 has compromised domains to use for C2. https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2021/03/04/goldmax-goldfinder-sibot-analyzing-nobelium-malware/
APT29 can create new users through Azure AD. https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2021/10/25/nobelium-targeting-delegated-administrative-privileges-to-facilitate-broader-attacks/

APT29 used account credentials they obtained to attempt access to Group Managed Service Account (gMSA) passwords. https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2021/01/20/deep-dive-into-the-solorigate-second-stage-activation-from-sunburst-to-teardrop-and-raindrop/
APT29 has stolen user's saved passwords from Chrome. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/observations-from-the-stellarparticle-campaign/

APT29 has accessed victims’ internal knowledge repositories (wikis) to view sensitive corporate information on products, services, and internal business operations. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/observations-from-the-stellarparticle-campaign/
APT29 has downloaded source code from code repositories. https://msrc-blog.microsoft.com/2021/02/18/microsoft-internal-solorigate-investigation-final-update/
APT29 has extracted files from compromised networks. https://www.volexity.com/blog/2020/12/14/dark-halo-leverages-solarwinds-compromise-to-breach-organizations/
APT29 has used steganography to hide C2 communications in images. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/ESET_Operation_Ghost_Dukes.pdf
APT29 staged data and files in password-protected archives on a victim's OWA server. https://www.volexity.com/blog/2020/12/14/dark-halo-leverages-solarwinds-compromise-to-breach-organizations/
APT29 used 7-Zip to decode its Raindrop malware. https://symantec-enterprise-blogs.security.com/blogs/threat-intelligence/solarwinds-raindrop-malware

APT29 has leveraged numerous pieces of malware that appear to be unique to APT29 and were likely developed for or by the group.   https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2020/12/evasive-attacker-leverages-solarwinds-supply-chain-compromises-with-sunburst-backdoor.html
APT29 has created self-signed digital certificates to enable mutual TLS authentication for malware.  https://www.pwc.co.uk/issues/cyber-security-services/insights/cleaning-up-after-wellmess.html

APT29 changed domain federation trust settings using Azure AD administrative permissions to configure the domain to accept authorization tokens signed by their own SAML signing certificate.  https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2020/12/28/using-microsoft-365-defender-to-coordinate-protection-against-solorigate/

APT29 used the Get-AcceptedDomain PowerShell cmdlet to enumerate accepted domains through an Exchange Management Shell.  They also used AdFind to enumerate domains and to discover trust between federated domains.  https://www.volexity.com/blog/2020/12/14/dark-halo-leverages-solarwinds-compromise-to-breach-organizations/

APT29 used dynamic DNS resolution to construct and resolve to randomly-generated subdomains for C2. https://www.volexity.com/blog/2020/12/14/dark-halo-leverages-solarwinds-compromise-to-breach-organizations/

APT29 collected emails from specific individuals, such as executives and IT staff, using New-MailboxExportRequest followed by Get-MailboxExportRequest.  https://www.volexity.com/blog/2020/12/14/dark-halo-leverages-solarwinds-compromise-to-breach-organizations/
APT29 has used multiple layers of encryption within malware to protect C2 communication. http://www.secureworks.com/research/threat-profiles/iron-hemlock
APT29 has used WMI event subscriptions for persistence.    http://www.slideshare.net/MatthewDunwoody1/no-easy-breach-derby-con-2016
APT29 used sticky-keys to obtain unauthenticated, privileged console access.  http://www.slideshare.net/MatthewDunwoody1/no-easy-breach-derby-con-2016

APT29 has exfiltrated collected data over a simple HTTPS request to a password-protected archive staged on a victim's OWA servers. https://www.volexity.com/blog/2020/12/14/dark-halo-leverages-solarwinds-compromise-to-breach-organizations/

APT29 has exploited CVE-2019-19781 for Citrix, CVE-2019-11510 for Pulse Secure VPNs, CVE-2018-13379 for FortiGate VPNs, and CVE-2019-9670 in Zimbra software to gain access. They have also exploited CVE-2020-0688 against the Microsoft Exchange Control Panel to regain access to a network.   https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/files/Advisory-APT29-targets-COVID-19-vaccine-development-V1-1.pdf

APT29 has used multiple software exploits for common client software, like Microsoft Word, Exchange, and Adobe Reader, to gain code execution.   https://www.f-secure.com/documents/996508/1030745/dukes_whitepaper.pdf
APT29 has exploited CVE-2021-36934 to escalate privileges on a compromised host. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/eset_threat_report_t32021.pdf

APT29 has used compromised identities to access networks via SSH, VPNs, and other remote access tools.   https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2021/03/04/goldmax-goldfinder-sibot-analyzing-nobelium-malware/

APT29 obtained information about the configured Exchange virtual directory using Get-WebServicesVirtualDirectory. https://www.volexity.com/blog/2020/12/14/dark-halo-leverages-solarwinds-compromise-to-breach-organizations/

APT29 has bypassed MFA set on OWA accounts by generating a cookie value from a previously stolen secret key. https://www.volexity.com/blog/2020/12/14/dark-halo-leverages-solarwinds-compromise-to-breach-organizations/
APT29 created tokens using compromised SAML signing certificates.  https://msrc-blog.microsoft.com/2020/12/13/customer-guidance-on-recent-nation-state-cyber-attacks/
APT29 has conducted credential theft operations to obtain credentials to be used for access to victim environments. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/observations-from-the-stellarparticle-campaign/

APT29 used the service control manager on a remote system to disable services associated with security monitoring products. https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2021/01/20/deep-dive-into-the-solorigate-second-stage-activation-from-sunburst-to-teardrop-and-raindrop/

APT29 used AUDITPOL to prevent the collection of audit logs. https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2021/01/20/deep-dive-into-the-solorigate-second-stage-activation-from-sunburst-to-teardrop-and-raindrop/

APT29 used netsh to configure firewall rules that limited certain UDP outbound packets. https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2021/01/20/deep-dive-into-the-solorigate-second-stage-activation-from-sunburst-to-teardrop-and-raindrop/

APT29 temporarily replaced legitimate utilities with their own, executed their payload, and then restored the original file. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2020/12/evasive-attacker-leverages-solarwinds-supply-chain-compromises-with-sunburst-backdoor.html

APT29 routinely removed their tools, including custom backdoors, once remote access was achieved. APT29 has also used SDelete to remove artifacts from victims.  https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2020/12/evasive-attacker-leverages-solarwinds-supply-chain-compromises-with-sunburst-backdoor.html

APT29 modified timestamps of backdoors to match legitimate Windows files. https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2021/01/20/deep-dive-into-the-solorigate-second-stage-activation-from-sunburst-to-teardrop-and-raindrop/
APT29 removed evidence of email export requests using Remove-MailboxExportRequest. https://www.volexity.com/blog/2020/12/14/dark-halo-leverages-solarwinds-compromise-to-breach-organizations/

APT29 has downloaded additional tools, such as TEARDROP malware and Cobalt Strike, to a compromised host following initial access. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2020/12/evasive-attacker-leverages-solarwinds-supply-chain-compromises-with-sunburst-backdoor.html

APT29 has set the hostnames of its C2 infrastructure to match legitimate hostnames in the victim environment. They have also used IP addresses originating from the same country as the victim for their VPN infrastructure. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2020/12/evasive-attacker-leverages-solarwinds-supply-chain-compromises-with-sunburst-backdoor.html

APT29 named tasks \Microsoft\Windows\SoftwareProtectionPlatform\EventCacheManager in order to appear legitimate. https://www.volexity.com/blog/2020/12/14/dark-halo-leverages-solarwinds-compromise-to-breach-organizations/
APT29 renamed software and DLL's with legitimate names to appear benign.   https://www.volexity.com/blog/2020/12/14/dark-halo-leverages-solarwinds-compromise-to-breach-organizations/

APT29 has edited the Microsoft.IdentityServer.Servicehost.exe.config file to load a malicious DLL into the AD FS process, thereby enabling persistent access to any service federated with AD FS for a user with a specified User Principal Name. https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2022/08/24/magicweb-nobeliums-post-compromise-trick-to-authenticate-as-anyone/
APT29 has used repeated MFA requests to gain access to victim accounts. https://www.mandiant.com/resources/russian-targeting-gov-business
APT29 has used TCP for C2 communications. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2018/11/not-so-cozy-an-uncomfortable-examination-of-a-suspected-apt29-phishing-campaign.html
APT29 has used encoded PowerShell commands. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2018/11/not-so-cozy-an-uncomfortable-examination-of-a-suspected-apt29-phishing-campaign.html
APT29 has used large file sizes to avoid detection. https://labs.sentinelone.com/noblebaron-new-poisoned-installers-could-be-used-in-supply-chain-attacks/
APT29 used UPX to pack files. http://www.slideshare.net/MatthewDunwoody1/no-easy-breach-derby-con-2016

APT29 has embedded an ISO file within an HTML attachment that contained JavaScript code to initiate malware execution. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/eset_threat_report_t32021.pdf
APT29 has obtained and used a variety of tools including Mimikatz, SDelete, Tor, meek, and Cobalt Strike.   http://www.slideshare.net/MatthewDunwoody1/no-easy-breach-derby-con-2016

APT29 leveraged privileged accounts to replicate directory service data with domain controllers.   https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2020/12/28/using-microsoft-365-defender-to-coordinate-protection-against-solorigate/

APT29 used the Get-ManagementRoleAssignment PowerShell cmdlet to enumerate Exchange management role assignments through an Exchange Management Shell. https://www.volexity.com/blog/2020/12/14/dark-halo-leverages-solarwinds-compromise-to-breach-organizations/
APT29 has used AdFind to enumerate domain groups. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/observations-from-the-stellarparticle-campaign/
APT29 has used spearphishing emails with an attachment to deliver files with exploits to initial victims.      https://www.f-secure.com/documents/996508/1030745/dukes_whitepaper.pdf
APT29 has used spearphishing with a link to trick victims into clicking on a link to a zip file containing malicious files.   http://www.slideshare.net/MatthewDunwoody1/no-easy-breach-derby-con-2016
APT29 has used the legitimate mailing service Constant Contact to send phishing e-mails. https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/files/Advisory-further-TTPs-associated-with-SVR-cyber-actors.pdf
APT29 has used multiple command-line utilities to enumerate running processes.   https://www.volexity.com/blog/2020/12/14/dark-halo-leverages-solarwinds-compromise-to-breach-organizations/

APT29 has used SSH port forwarding capabilities on public-facing systems, and configured at least one instance of Cobalt Strike to use a network pipe over SMB during the 2020 SolarWinds intrusion.  https://symantec-enterprise-blogs.security.com/blogs/threat-intelligence/solarwinds-raindrop-malware

A backdoor used by APT29 created a Tor hidden service to forward traffic from the Tor client to local ports 3389 (RDP), 139 (Netbios), and 445 (SMB) enabling full remote access from outside the network and has also used TOR.  http://www.slideshare.net/MatthewDunwoody1/no-easy-breach-derby-con-2016
APT29 has used the meek domain fronting plugin for Tor to hide the destination of C2 traffic. http://www.slideshare.net/MatthewDunwoody1/no-easy-breach-derby-con-2016
APT29 has used RDP sessions from public-facing systems to internal servers. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/observations-from-the-stellarparticle-campaign/
APT29 has used administrative accounts to connect over SMB to targeted users. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/observations-from-the-stellarparticle-campaign/
APT29 has used WinRM via PowerShell to execute command and payloads on remote hosts. https://symantec-enterprise-blogs.security.com/blogs/threat-intelligence/solarwinds-raindrop-malware
APT29 has used AdFind to enumerate remote systems. https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2021/01/20/deep-dive-into-the-solorigate-second-stage-activation-from-sunburst-to-teardrop-and-raindrop/

APT29 used scheduler and schtasks to create new tasks on remote hosts as part of lateral movement.  They have manipulated scheduled tasks by updating an existing legitimate task to execute their tools and then returned the scheduled task to its original configuration.  APT29 also created a scheduled task to maintain SUNSPOT persistence when the host booted during the 2020 SolarWinds intrusion.  They previously used named and hijacked scheduled tasks to also establish persistence. https://www.volexity.com/blog/2020/12/14/dark-halo-leverages-solarwinds-compromise-to-breach-organizations/
APT29 has installed web shells on exploited Microsoft Exchange servers. https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/files/Advisory-further-TTPs-associated-with-SVR-cyber-actors.pdf

APT29 has abused misconfigured AD CS certificate templates to impersonate admin users and create additional authentication certificates. https://www.mandiant.com/resources/tracking-apt29-phishing-campaigns

APT29 obtained Ticket Granting Service (TGS) tickets for Active Directory Service Principle Names to crack offline. https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2021/01/20/deep-dive-into-the-solorigate-second-stage-activation-from-sunburst-to-teardrop-and-raindrop/
APT29 has stolen Chrome browser cookies by copying the Chrome profile directories of targeted users. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/observations-from-the-stellarparticle-campaign/

APT29 was able to get SUNBURST signed by SolarWinds code signing certificates by injecting the malware into the SolarWinds Orion software lifecycle. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2020/12/evasive-attacker-leverages-solarwinds-supply-chain-compromises-with-sunburst-backdoor.html
APT29 has embedded ISO images and VHDX files in HTML to evade Mark-of-the-Web. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/eset_threat_report_t32021.pdf

APT29 gained initial network access to some victims via a trojanized update of SolarWinds Orion software.    https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2020/12/evasive-attacker-leverages-solarwinds-supply-chain-compromises-with-sunburst-backdoor.html
APT29 has use mshta to execute malicious scripts on a compromised host. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/eset_threat_report_t32021.pdf
APT29 has used Rundll32.exe to execute payloads.   https://msrc-blog.microsoft.com/2020/12/13/customer-guidance-on-recent-nation-state-cyber-attacks/

APT29 used fsutil to check available free space before executing actions that might create large files on disk. https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2021/01/20/deep-dive-into-the-solorigate-second-stage-activation-from-sunburst-to-teardrop-and-raindrop/

APT29 has used GoldFinder to perform HTTP GET requests to check internet connectivity and identify HTTP proxy servers and other redirectors that an HTTP request travels through. https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2021/03/04/goldmax-goldfinder-sibot-analyzing-nobelium-malware/

APT29 has gained access through compromised accounts at cloud solution partners, and used compromised certificates issued by Mimecast to authenticate to Mimecast customer systems.   https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/files/Advisory-further-TTPs-associated-with-SVR-cyber-actors.pdf

APT29 obtained PKI keys, certificate files and the private encryption key from an Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS) container to decrypt corresponding SAML signing certificates.  https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2020/12/28/using-microsoft-365-defender-to-coordinate-protection-against-solorigate/

APT29 used forged SAML tokens that allowed the actors to impersonate users and bypass MFA, enabling APT29 to access enterprise cloud applications and services.  https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2020/12/28/using-microsoft-365-defender-to-coordinate-protection-against-solorigate/
APT29 has used compromised service principals to make changes to the Office 365 environment. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/observations-from-the-stellarparticle-campaign/
APT29 used Kerberos ticket attacks for lateral movement. http://www.slideshare.net/MatthewDunwoody1/no-easy-breach-derby-con-2016

APT29 used stolen cookies to access cloud resources, and a forged duo-sid cookie to bypass MFA set on an email account.  https://www.volexity.com/blog/2020/12/14/dark-halo-leverages-solarwinds-compromise-to-breach-organizations/

APT29 has used various forms of spearphishing attempting to get a user to click on a malicous link.    https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2018/11/not-so-cozy-an-uncomfortable-examination-of-a-suspected-apt29-phishing-campaign.html

APT29 has used various forms of spearphishing attempting to get a user to open attachments, including, but not limited to, malicious Microsoft Word documents, .pdf, and .lnk files.       https://www.f-secure.com/documents/996508/1030745/dukes_whitepaper.pdf

APT29 used different compromised credentials for remote access and to move laterally.   https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2020/12/evasive-attacker-leverages-solarwinds-supply-chain-compromises-with-sunburst-backdoor.html

APT29 has used valid accounts, including administrator accounts, to help facilitate lateral movement on compromised networks.   https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/ESET_Operation_Ghost_Dukes.pdf
APT29 has used compromised local accounts to access victims' networks. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/observations-from-the-stellarparticle-campaign/
APT29 has used a compromised O365 administrator account to create a new Service Principal. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/observations-from-the-stellarparticle-campaign/
APT29 has used social media platforms to hide communications to C2 servers. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/ESET_Operation_Ghost_Dukes.pdf

APT29 used WMI to steal credentials and execute backdoors at a future time.  They have also used WMI for the remote execution of files for lateral movement.  http://www.slideshare.net/MatthewDunwoody1/no-easy-breach-derby-con-2016

APT3 has been known to add created accounts to local admin groups to maintain elevated access. http://carnal0wnage.attackresearch.com/2012/09/more-on-aptsim.html
APT3 has used tools to compress data before exfilling it. http://carnal0wnage.attackresearch.com/2012/09/more-on-aptsim.html
APT3 places scripts in the startup folder for persistence. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2014/11/operation_doubletap.html
APT3 has been known to brute force password hashes to be able to leverage plain text credentials. https://attack.mitre.org/docs/APT3_Adversary_Emulation_Plan.pdf
APT3 has used PowerShell on victim systems to download and run payloads after exploitation. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2014/11/operation_doubletap.html

An APT3 downloader uses the Windows command "cmd.exe" /C whoami. The group also uses a tool to execute commands on remote computers.  https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2014/11/operation_doubletap.html
APT3 has been known to create or enable accounts, such as support_388945a0. http://carnal0wnage.attackresearch.com/2012/09/more-on-aptsim.html
APT3 has a tool that creates a new service for persistence. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2014/11/operation_doubletap.html
APT3 has used tools to dump passwords from browsers. http://www.symantec.com/connect/blogs/buckeye-cyberespionage-group-shifts-gaze-us-hong-kong
APT3 will identify Microsoft Office documents on the victim's computer. http://carnal0wnage.attackresearch.com/2012/09/more-on-aptsim.html
APT3 has been known to stage files for exfiltration in a single location. http://carnal0wnage.attackresearch.com/2012/09/more-on-aptsim.html
APT3 replaces the Sticky Keys binary C:\Windows\System32\sethc.exe for persistence. http://carnal0wnage.attackresearch.com/2012/09/more-on-aptsim.html

APT3 has a tool that exfiltrates data over the C2 channel. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2014/04/new-zero-day-exploit-targeting-internet-explorer-versions-9-through-11-identified-in-targeted-attacks.html

APT3 has exploited the Adobe Flash Player vulnerability CVE-2015-3113 and Internet Explorer vulnerability CVE-2014-1776.  https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2015/06/operation-clandestine-wolf-adobe-flash-zero-day.html

APT3 has a tool that looks for files and directories on the local file system.  https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2014/04/new-zero-day-exploit-targeting-internet-explorer-versions-9-through-11-identified-in-targeted-attacks.html
APT3 has been known to use -WindowStyle Hidden to conceal PowerShell windows. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2014/11/operation_doubletap.html

APT3 has been known to side load DLLs with a valid version of Chrome with one of their tools.  https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2014/04/new-zero-day-exploit-targeting-internet-explorer-versions-9-through-11-identified-in-targeted-attacks.html
APT3 has a tool that can delete files. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2014/04/new-zero-day-exploit-targeting-internet-explorer-versions-9-through-11-identified-in-targeted-attacks.html

APT3 has a tool that can copy files to remote machines. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2014/04/new-zero-day-exploit-targeting-internet-explorer-versions-9-through-11-identified-in-targeted-attacks.html
APT3 has used a keylogging tool that records keystrokes in encrypted files. http://www.symantec.com/connect/blogs/buckeye-cyberespionage-group-shifts-gaze-us-hong-kong

An APT3 downloader first establishes a SOCKS5 connection to 192.157.198[.]103 using TCP port 1913; once the server response is verified, it then requests a connection to 192.184.60[.]229 on TCP port 81. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2014/11/operation_doubletap.html
An APT3 downloader establishes SOCKS5 connections for its initial C2. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2014/11/operation_doubletap.html
APT3 obfuscates files or information to help evade defensive measures. http://www.symantec.com/connect/blogs/buckeye-cyberespionage-group-shifts-gaze-us-hong-kong
APT3 has been known to pack their tools.  https://attack.mitre.org/docs/APT3_Adversary_Emulation_Plan.pdf
APT3 has been known to remove indicators of compromise from tools. https://attack.mitre.org/docs/APT3_Adversary_Emulation_Plan.pdf

APT3 has used a tool to dump credentials by injecting itself into lsass.exe and triggering with the argument "dig." http://www.symantec.com/connect/blogs/buckeye-cyberespionage-group-shifts-gaze-us-hong-kong
APT3 has a tool that can enumerate the permissions associated with Windows groups. http://www.symantec.com/connect/blogs/buckeye-cyberespionage-group-shifts-gaze-us-hong-kong
APT3 has sent spearphishing emails containing malicious links. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2015/06/operation-clandestine-wolf-adobe-flash-zero-day.html

APT3 has a tool that can list out currently running processes.  https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2014/04/new-zero-day-exploit-targeting-internet-explorer-versions-9-through-11-identified-in-targeted-attacks.html
An APT3 downloader establishes SOCKS5 connections for its initial C2. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2014/11/operation_doubletap.html

APT3 enables the Remote Desktop Protocol for persistence.  APT3 has also interacted with compromised systems to browse and copy files through RDP sessions. http://carnal0wnage.attackresearch.com/2012/09/more-on-aptsim.html
APT3 will copy files over to Windows Admin Shares (like ADMIN$) as part of lateral movement. http://www.symantec.com/connect/blogs/buckeye-cyberespionage-group-shifts-gaze-us-hong-kong
APT3 has a tool that can detect the existence of remote systems.  http://www.symantec.com/connect/blogs/buckeye-cyberespionage-group-shifts-gaze-us-hong-kong

An APT3 downloader creates persistence by creating the following scheduled task: schtasks /create /tn "mysc" /tr C:\Users\Public\test.exe /sc ONLOGON /ru "System". https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2014/11/operation_doubletap.html
APT3 has a tool that can run DLLs. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2014/04/new-zero-day-exploit-targeting-internet-explorer-versions-9-through-11-identified-in-targeted-attacks.html
APT3 has a tool that can obtain information about the local system.  http://www.symantec.com/connect/blogs/buckeye-cyberespionage-group-shifts-gaze-us-hong-kong

A keylogging tool used by APT3 gathers network information from the victim, including the MAC address, IP address, WINS, DHCP server, and gateway.  http://www.symantec.com/connect/blogs/buckeye-cyberespionage-group-shifts-gaze-us-hong-kong
APT3 has a tool that can enumerate current network connections.   http://www.symantec.com/connect/blogs/buckeye-cyberespionage-group-shifts-gaze-us-hong-kong

An APT3 downloader uses the Windows command "cmd.exe" /C whoami to verify that it is running with the elevated privileges of "System." https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2014/11/operation_doubletap.html

APT3 has a tool that can locate credentials in files on the file system such as those from Firefox or Chrome. http://www.symantec.com/connect/blogs/buckeye-cyberespionage-group-shifts-gaze-us-hong-kong
APT3 has lured victims into clicking malicious links delivered through spearphishing. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2015/06/operation-clandestine-wolf-adobe-flash-zero-day.html
APT3 leverages valid accounts after gaining credentials for use within the victim domain. http://www.symantec.com/connect/blogs/buckeye-cyberespionage-group-shifts-gaze-us-hong-kong

APT32 has set up and operated websites to gather information and deliver malware. https://www.volexity.com/blog/2020/11/06/oceanlotus-extending-cyber-espionage-operations-through-fake-websites/
APT32 has set up Dropbox, Amazon S3, and Google Drive to host malicious downloads. https://www.volexity.com/blog/2020/11/06/oceanlotus-extending-cyber-espionage-operations-through-fake-websites/

APT32 has used JavaScript that communicates over HTTP or HTTPS to attacker controlled domains to download additional frameworks. APT32 established persistence using Registry Run keys, both to execute PowerShell and VBS scripts as well as to execute their backdoor directly.   https://www.cybereason.com/blog/operation-cobalt-kitty-apt
APT32 has used COM scriptlets to download Cobalt Strike beacons. https://cdn2.hubspot.net/hubfs/3354902/Cybereason%20Labs%20Analysis%20Operation%20Cobalt%20Kitty.pdf
APT32 has used PowerShell-based tools, PowerShell one-liners, and shellcode loaders for execution.   https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2017/05/cyber-espionage-apt32.html
APT32 has used cmd.exe for execution. https://cdn2.hubspot.net/hubfs/3354902/Cybereason%20Labs%20Analysis%20Operation%20Cobalt%20Kitty.pdf
APT32 has used macros, COM scriptlets, and VBS scripts.  https://www.cybereason.com/blog/operation-cobalt-kitty-apt
APT32 has used JavaScript for drive-by downloads and C2 communications.  https://cdn2.hubspot.net/hubfs/3354902/Cybereason%20Labs%20Analysis%20Operation%20Cobalt%20Kitty.pdf

APT32 modified Windows Services to ensure PowerShell scripts were loaded on the system. APT32 also creates a Windows service to establish persistence.   https://www.welivesecurity.com/2018/03/13/oceanlotus-ships-new-backdoor/
APT32 has infected victims by tricking them into visiting compromised watering hole websites.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/2018/03/13/oceanlotus-ships-new-backdoor/
APT32 has set up Facebook pages in tandem with fake websites. https://www.volexity.com/blog/2020/11/06/oceanlotus-extending-cyber-espionage-operations-through-fake-websites/

APT32's backdoor has exfiltrated data using the already opened channel with its C&C server. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2019/03/20/fake-or-fake-keeping-up-with-oceanlotus-decoys/
APT32 has used RTF document that includes an exploit to execute malicious code. (CVE-2017-11882) https://www.welivesecurity.com/2019/03/20/fake-or-fake-keeping-up-with-oceanlotus-decoys/
APT32 has used CVE-2016-7255 to escalate privileges. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2017/05/cyber-espionage-apt32.html
APT32's backdoor possesses the capability to list files and directories on a machine.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/2019/03/20/fake-or-fake-keeping-up-with-oceanlotus-decoys/
APT32's macOS backdoor changes the permission of the file it wants to execute to 755. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2019/04/09/oceanlotus-macos-malware-update/

APT32 has conducted targeted surveillance against activists and bloggers. https://www.amnestyusa.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/Click-and-Bait_Vietnamese-Human-Rights-Defenders-Targeted-with-Spyware-Attacks.pdf

APT32 has collected e-mail addresses for activists and bloggers in order to target them with spyware. https://www.amnestyusa.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/Click-and-Bait_Vietnamese-Human-Rights-Defenders-Targeted-with-Spyware-Attacks.pdf
APT32's macOS backdoor hides the clientID file via a chflags function. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2019/04/09/oceanlotus-macos-malware-update/
APT32 has used the WindowStyle parameter to conceal PowerShell windows.    https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2017/05/cyber-espionage-apt32.html
APT32 used NTFS alternate data streams to hide their payloads. https://cdn2.hubspot.net/hubfs/3354902/Cybereason%20Labs%20Analysis%20Operation%20Cobalt%20Kitty.pdf

APT32 ran legitimately-signed executables from Symantec and McAfee which load a malicious DLL. The group also side-loads its backdoor by dropping a library and a legitimate, signed executable (AcroTranscoder).   https://www.cybereason.com/blog/operation-cobalt-kitty-apt
APT32 has cleared select event log entries. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2017/05/cyber-espionage-apt32.html
APT32's macOS backdoor can receive a "delete" command. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2019/04/09/oceanlotus-macos-malware-update/

APT32 has used scheduled task raw XML with a backdated timestamp of June 2, 2016. The group has also set the creation time of the files dropped by the second stage of the exploit to match the creation time of kernel32.dll. Use: APT37 has a function in the initial dropper to bypass Windows UAC in order to execute the next payload with higher privileges. https://securelist.com/scarcruft-continues-to-evolve-introduces-bluetooth-harvester/90729/
APT37 uses HTTPS to conceal C2 communications. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/2018/01/korea-in-crosshairs.html
APT37 has used an audio capturing utility known as SOUNDWAVE that captures microphone input. https://www2.fireeye.com/rs/848-DID-242/images/rpt_APT37.pdf
APT37's has added persistence via the Registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\CurrentVersion\Run\.  https://www2.fireeye.com/rs/848-DID-242/images/rpt_APT37.pdf
APT37 has used Ruby scripts to execute payloads. https://www.volexity.com/blog/2021/08/24/north-korean-bluelight-special-inkysquid-deploys-rokrat/
APT37 has used the command-line interface.  https://www2.fireeye.com/rs/848-DID-242/images/rpt_APT37.pdf
APT37 executes shellcode and a VBA script to decode Base64 strings. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/2018/01/korea-in-crosshairs.html
APT37 has used Python scripts to execute payloads. https://www.volexity.com/blog/2021/08/24/north-korean-bluelight-special-inkysquid-deploys-rokrat/
APT37 has used a credential stealer known as ZUMKONG that can harvest usernames and passwords stored in browsers. https://www2.fireeye.com/rs/848-DID-242/images/rpt_APT37.pdf
APT37 has collected data from victims' local systems. https://www2.fireeye.com/rs/848-DID-242/images/rpt_APT37.pdf
APT37 has access to destructive malware that is capable of overwriting a machine's Master Boot Record (MBR).  https://www2.fireeye.com/rs/848-DID-242/images/rpt_APT37.pdf

APT37 has used strategic web compromises, particularly of South Korean websites, to distribute malware. The group has also used torrent file-sharing sites to more indiscriminately disseminate malware to victims. As part of their compromises, the group has used a Javascript based profiler called RICECURRY to profile a victim's web browser and deliver malicious code accordingly.   https://securelist.com/operation-daybreak/75100/

APT37 has used exploits for Flash Player (CVE-2016-4117, CVE-2018-4878), Word (CVE-2017-0199), Internet Explorer (CVE-2020-1380 and CVE-2020-26411), and Microsoft Edge (CVE-2021-26411) for execution.    https://securelist.com/operation-daybreak/75100/
APT37 has downloaded second stage malware from compromised websites.    https://www2.fireeye.com/rs/848-DID-242/images/rpt_APT37.pdf
APT37 has used Windows DDE for execution of commands and a malicious VBS. https://securelist.com/operation-daybreak/75100/
APT37 has signed its malware with an invalid digital certificates listed as "Tencent Technology (Shenzhen) Company Limited." https://securelist.com/operation-daybreak/75100/
APT37 leverages the Windows API calls: VirtualAlloc(), WriteProcessMemory(), and CreateRemoteThread() for process injection. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/2018/01/korea-in-crosshairs.html
APT37 obfuscates strings and payloads.   https://blog.talosintelligence.com/2018/01/korea-in-crosshairs.html
APT37 uses steganography to send images to users that are embedded with shellcode.  https://blog.talosintelligence.com/2018/01/korea-in-crosshairs.html

APT37 has a Bluetooth device harvester, which uses Windows Bluetooth APIs to find information on connected Bluetooth devices.  https://securelist.com/scarcruft-continues-to-evolve-introduces-bluetooth-harvester/90729/
APT37 delivers malware using spearphishing emails with malicious HWP attachments.   https://www2.fireeye.com/rs/848-DID-242/images/rpt_APT37.pdf
APT37's Freenki malware lists running processes using the Microsoft Windows API. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/2018/01/korea-in-crosshairs.html
APT37 injects its malware variant, ROKRAT, into the cmd.exe process. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/2018/01/korea-in-crosshairs.html
APT37 has created scheduled tasks to run malicious scripts on a compromised host. https://www.volexity.com/blog/2021/08/24/north-korean-bluelight-special-inkysquid-deploys-rokrat/
APT37 collects the computer name, the BIOS model, and execution path. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/2018/01/korea-in-crosshairs.html
APT37 identifies the victim username. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/2018/01/korea-in-crosshairs.html
APT37 has used malware that will issue the command shutdown /r /t 1 to reboot a system after wiping its MBR. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/2018/01/korea-in-crosshairs.html
APT37 has sent spearphishing attachments attempting to get a user to open them. https://www2.fireeye.com/rs/848-DID-242/images/rpt_APT37.pdf
APT37 leverages social networking sites and cloud platforms (AOL, Twitter, Yandex, Mediafire, pCloud, Dropbox, and Box) for C2.  https://www2.fireeye.com/rs/848-DID-242/images/rpt_APT37.pdf

Use: APT38 used a backdoor, QUICKRIDE, to communicate to the C2 server over HTTP and HTTPS. https://content.fireeye.com/apt/rpt-apt38

APT38 has collected browser bookmark information to learn more about compromised hosts, obtain personal information about users, and acquire details about internal network resources. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-239a
APT38 has used brute force techniques to attempt account access when passwords are unknown or when password hashes are unavailable. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-239a
APT38 used a Trojan called KEYLIME to collect data from the clipboard. https://content.fireeye.com/apt/rpt-apt38
APT38 has used PowerShell to execute commands and other operational tasks. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-239a
APT38 has used a command-line tunneler, NACHOCHEESE, to give them shell access to a victim’s machine. https://content.fireeye.com/apt/rpt-apt38
APT38 has used VBScript to execute commands and other operational tasks. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-239a
APT38 has installed a new Windows service to establish persistence. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-239a
APT38 has used a custom secure delete function to make deleted files unrecoverable. https://content.fireeye.com/apt/rpt-apt38
APT38 has used Hermes ransomware to encrypt files with AES256. https://content.fireeye.com/apt/rpt-apt38
APT38 has collected data from a compromised host. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-239a
APT38 has used DYEPACK to create, delete, and alter records in databases used for SWIFT transactions. https://content.fireeye.com/apt/rpt-apt38
APT38 has used DYEPACK to manipulate SWIFT messages en route to a printer. https://content.fireeye.com/apt/rpt-apt38

APT38 has used DYEPACK.FOX to manipulate PDF data as it is accessed to remove traces of fraudulent SWIFT transactions from the data displayed to the end user. https://content.fireeye.com/apt/rpt-apt38
APT38 has used a custom MBR wiper named BOOTWRECK to render systems inoperable. https://content.fireeye.com/apt/rpt-apt38
APT38 has conducted watering holes schemes to gain initial access to victims.  https://content.fireeye.com/apt/rpt-apt38
APT38 have enumerated files and directories, or searched in specific locations within a compromised host. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-239a
APT38 has prepended a space to all of their terminal commands to operate without leaving traces in the HISTCONTROL environment. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-239a
APT38 have created firewall exemptions on specific ports, including ports 443, 6443, 8443, and 9443. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-239a
APT38 clears Window Event logs and Sysmon logs from the system. https://content.fireeye.com/apt/rpt-apt38

APT38 has used a utility called CLOSESHAVE that can securely delete a file from the system. They have also removed malware, tools, or other non-native files used during the intrusion to reduce their footprint or as part of the post-intrusion cleanup process.  https://content.fireeye.com/apt/rpt-apt38
APT38 has modified data timestamps to mimic files that are in the same folder on a compromised host. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-239a
APT38 used a backdoor, NESTEGG, that has the capability to download and upload files to and from a victim’s machine. https://content.fireeye.com/apt/rpt-apt38
APT38 used a Trojan called KEYLIME to capture keystrokes from the victim’s machine. https://content.fireeye.com/apt/rpt-apt38
APT38 uses a tool called CLEANTOAD that has the capability to modify Registry keys. https://content.fireeye.com/apt/rpt-apt38
APT38 has used the Windows API to execute code within a victim's system. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-239a
APT38 has enumerated network shares on a compromised host. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-239a
APT38 has used several code packing methods such as Themida, Enigma, VMProtect, and Obsidium, to pack their implants. https://content.fireeye.com/apt/rpt-apt38
APT38 has obtained and used open-source tools such as Mimikatz. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2018/04/03/lazarus-killdisk-central-american-casino/
APT38 has conducted spearphishing campaigns using malicious email attachments. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-239a
APT38 leveraged Sysmon to understand the processes, services in the organization. https://content.fireeye.com/apt/rpt-apt38
APT38 has used cron to create pre-scheduled and periodic background jobs on a Linux system. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-239a
APT38 has used Task Scheduler to run programs at system startup or on a scheduled basis for persistence. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-239a
APT38 has used web shells for persistence or to ensure redundant access. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-239a
APT38 has identified security software, configurations, defensive tools, and sensors installed on a compromised system. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-239a
APT38 has used CHM files to move concealed payloads. https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/43/2018/03/07180244/Lazarus_Under_The_Hood_PDF_final.pdf
APT38 has used rundll32.exe to execute binaries, scripts, and Control Panel Item files and to execute code via proxy to avoid triggering security tools. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-239a
APT38 has attempted to get detailed information about a compromised host, including the operating system, version, patches, hotfixes, and service packs. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-239a
APT38 installed a port monitoring tool, MAPMAKER, to print the active TCP connections on the local system. https://content.fireeye.com/apt/rpt-apt38
APT38 has identified primary users, currently logged in users, sets of users that commonly use a system, or inactive users. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-239a
APT38 has created new services or modified existing ones to run executables, commands, or scripts. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-239a
APT38 has used a custom MBR wiper named BOOTWRECK, which will initiate a system reboot after wiping the victim's MBR. https://content.fireeye.com/apt/rpt-apt38
APT38 has attempted to lure victims into enabling malicious macros within email attachments. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-239a

BackdoorDiplomacy has used SMBTouch, a vulnerability scanner, to determine whether a target is vulnerable to EternalBlue malware. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2021/06/10/backdoordiplomacy-upgrading-quarian-turian/

BackdoorDiplomacy has used NetCat and PortQry to enumerate network connections and display the status of related TCP and UDP ports. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2021/06/10/backdoordiplomacy-upgrading-quarian-turian/

Use: FIN8 has used a malicious framework designed to impersonate the lsass.exe/vmtoolsd.exe token. https://businessinsights.bitdefender.com/deep-dive-into-a-fin8-attack-a-forensic-investigation
FIN8 has used HTTPS for command and control. https://businessinsights.bitdefender.com/deep-dive-into-a-fin8-attack-a-forensic-investigation
FIN8 has used RAR to compress collected data before exfiltration. https://www2.fireeye.com/WBNR-Know-Your-Enemy-UNC622-Spear-Phishing.html

FIN8's malicious spearphishing payloads are executed as PowerShell. FIN8 has also used PowerShell for lateral movement and credential access.   https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2017/06/obfuscation-in-the-wild.html

FIN8 has used a Batch file to automate frequently executed post compromise cleanup activities.  FIN8 has also executed commands remotely via cmd.  https://www2.fireeye.com/WBNR-Know-Your-Enemy-UNC622-Spear-Phishing.html
FIN8 aggregates staged data from a network into a single location. https://www2.fireeye.com/WBNR-Know-Your-Enemy-UNC622-Spear-Phishing.html
FIN8 has retrieved a list of trusted domains by using Nltest.exe /domain_trusts. https://businessinsights.bitdefender.com/deep-dive-into-a-fin8-attack-a-forensic-investigation
FIN8 has used the Plink utility to tunnel RDP back to C2 infrastructure. https://www2.fireeye.com/WBNR-Know-Your-Enemy-UNC622-Spear-Phishing.html
FIN8 has used WMI event subscriptions for persistence. https://businessinsights.bitdefender.com/deep-dive-into-a-fin8-attack-a-forensic-investigation
FIN8 has used FTP to exfiltrate collected data. https://www2.fireeye.com/WBNR-Know-Your-Enemy-UNC622-Spear-Phishing.html
FIN8 has exploited the CVE-2016-0167 local vulnerability.  https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2016/05/windows-zero-day-payment-cards.html
FIN8 has cleared logs during post compromise cleanup activities. https://www2.fireeye.com/WBNR-Know-Your-Enemy-UNC622-Spear-Phishing.html
FIN8 has deleted tmp and prefetch files during post compromise cleanup activities. https://www2.fireeye.com/WBNR-Know-Your-Enemy-UNC622-Spear-Phishing.html
FIN8 has used remote code execution to download subsequent payloads.  https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2016/05/windows-zero-day-payment-cards.html
FIN8 has deleted Registry keys during post compromise cleanup activities. https://www2.fireeye.com/WBNR-Know-Your-Enemy-UNC622-Spear-Phishing.html

FIN8 has used environment variables and standard input (stdin) to obfuscate command-line arguments. FIN8 also obfuscates malicious macros delivered as payloads.   https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2017/06/obfuscation-in-the-wild.html
FIN8 harvests credentials using Invoke-Mimikatz or Windows Credentials Editor (WCE). https://www2.fireeye.com/WBNR-Know-Your-Enemy-UNC622-Spear-Phishing.html
FIN8 has distributed targeted emails containing Word documents with embedded malicious macros.   https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2017/06/obfuscation-in-the-wild.html
FIN8 has distributed targeted emails containing links to malicious documents with embedded macros. https://www2.fireeye.com/WBNR-Know-Your-Enemy-UNC622-Spear-Phishing.html
FIN8 has injected malicious code into a new svchost.exe process. https://businessinsights.bitdefender.com/deep-dive-into-a-fin8-attack-a-forensic-investigation
FIN8 has used RDP for lateral movement. https://www2.fireeye.com/WBNR-Know-Your-Enemy-UNC622-Spear-Phishing.html
FIN8 has attempted to map to C$ on enumerated hosts to test the scope of their current credentials/context. https://www2.fireeye.com/WBNR-Know-Your-Enemy-UNC622-Spear-Phishing.html

FIN8 has used dsquery and other Active Directory utilities to enumerate hosts; they have also used nltest.exe /dclist to retrieve a list of domain controllers.  https://www2.fireeye.com/WBNR-Know-Your-Enemy-UNC622-Spear-Phishing.html
FIN8 has used scheduled tasks to maintain RDP backdoors. https://www2.fireeye.com/WBNR-Know-Your-Enemy-UNC622-Spear-Phishing.html
FIN8 has used Registry keys to detect and avoid executing in potential sandboxes. https://www2.fireeye.com/WBNR-Know-Your-Enemy-UNC622-Spear-Phishing.html
FIN8 has used emails with malicious links to lure victims into installing malware.   https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2017/06/obfuscation-in-the-wild.html
FIN8 has used malicious e-mail attachments to lure victims into executing malware.   https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2017/06/obfuscation-in-the-wild.html
FIN8 has used valid accounts for persistence and lateral movement. https://www2.fireeye.com/WBNR-Know-Your-Enemy-UNC622-Spear-Phishing.html

FIN8 has used sslip.io, a free IP to domain mapping service that also makes SSL certificate generation easier for traffic encryption, as part of their command and control. https://businessinsights.bitdefender.com/deep-dive-into-a-fin8-attack-a-forensic-investigation

FIN8's malicious spearphishing payloads use WMI to launch malware and spawn cmd.exe execution. FIN8 has also used WMIC for lateral movement as well as during and post compromise cleanup activities.   https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2017/06/obfuscation-in-the-wild.html
