Use: Lazarus Group keylogger KiloAlfa obtains user tokens from interactive sessions to execute itself with API call CreateProcessAsUserA under that user's context.  https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf

Lazarus Group has queried an active directory server to obtain the list of accounts, including administrator accounts. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/ESET_Operation_Interception.pdf

Lazarus Group malware WhiskeyDelta-Two contains a function that attempts to rename the administrator’s account.  https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf
Lazarus Group has acquired domains related to their campaigns to act as distribution points and C2 channels.   https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa21-048a
Lazarus Group has acquired servers to host their malicious tools. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/ESET_Operation_Interception.pdf
Lazarus Group has hosted malicious downloads on Github and Dropbox.  https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa21-048a

Lazarus Group executed Responder using the command [Responder file path] -i [IP address] -rPv on a compromised host to harvest credentials and move laterally. https://securelist.com/lazarus-threatneedle/100803/
Lazarus Group has conducted C2 over HTTP and HTTPS.       https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/lazarus-resurfaces-targets-global-banks-bitcoin-users/

Lazarus Group malware IndiaIndia obtains and sends to its C2 server the title of the window for each running process. The KilaAlfa keylogger also reports the title of the window in the foreground.   https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf

Lazarus Group has compressed exfiltrated data with RAR and used RomeoDelta malware to archive specified directories in .zip format, encrypt the .zip file, and upload it to C2.     https://operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Loaders-Installers-and-Uninstallers-Report.pdf

Lazarus Group malware IndiaIndia saves information gathered about the victim to a file that is compressed with Zlib, encrypted, and uploaded to a C2 server.  https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-RAT-and-Staging-Report.pdf

A Lazarus Group malware sample encrypts data using a simple byte based XOR operation prior to exfiltration.    https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf

Lazarus Group has maintained persistence by loading malicious code into a startup folder or by adding a Registry Run key.     https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf

Lazarus Group malware has maintained persistence on a system by creating a LNK shortcut in the user’s Startup folder.  https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/lazarus-resurfaces-targets-global-banks-bitcoin-users/
Lazarus Group has performed brute force attacks against administrator accounts. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/ESET_Operation_Interception.pdf

Lazarus Group malware attempts to connect to Windows shares for lateral movement by using a generated list of usernames, which center around permutations of the username Administrator, and weak passwords.  https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf
Lazarus Group has used PowerShell to execute commands and malicious code.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/ESET_Operation_Interception.pdf

Lazarus Group malware uses cmd.exe to execute commands on a compromised host.      A Destover-like variant used by Lazarus Group uses a batch file mechanism to delete its binaries from the system. https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf

Lazarus Group has used VBA and embedded macros in Word documents to execute malicious code.    https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/operation-north-star-a-job-offer-thats-too-good-to-be-true/?hilite=%27Operation%27%2C%27North%27%2C%27Star%27
Lazarus Group has compromised legitimate domains, including those hosted in the US and Italy, for C2. https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/operation-north-star-behind-the-scenes/
Lazarus Group has compromised servers to stage malicious tools.    https://securelist.com/lazarus-threatneedle/100803/

Several Lazarus Group malware families install themselves as new services.  https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf

Lazarus Group has used a custom secure delete function to overwrite file contents with data from heap memory. https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf
A Lazarus Group malware sample encodes data with base64. https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/lazarus-resurfaces-targets-global-banks-bitcoin-users/

Lazarus Group has collected data and files from compromised networks.      https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf

Lazarus Group malware also uses a unique form of communication encryption known as FakeTLS that mimics TLS but uses a different encryption method, potentially evading SSL traffic inspection/decryption.    https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf

Lazarus Group malware IndiaIndia saves information gathered about the victim to a file that is saved in the %TEMP% directory, then compressed, encrypted, and uploaded to a C2 server.  https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf

Lazarus Group replaced the background wallpaper of systems with a threatening image after rendering the system unbootable with a Disk Structure Wipe. https://web.archive.org/web/20160303200515/https://operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Destructive-Malware-Report.pdf

Lazarus Group has used shellcode within macros to decrypt and manually map DLLs and shellcode into memory at runtime.  https://blog.malwarebytes.com/threat-intelligence/2022/01/north-koreas-lazarus-apt-leverages-windows-update-client-github-in-latest-campaign/
Lazarus Group has developed custom malware for use in their operations.    https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa21-048a

Lazarus Group has used malware like WhiskeyAlfa to overwrite the first 64MB of every drive with a mix of static and random buffers. A similar process is then used to wipe content in logical drives and, finally, attempt to wipe every byte of every sector on every drive. WhiskeyBravo can be used to overwrite the first 4.9MB of physical drives. WhiskeyDelta can overwrite the first 132MB or 1.5MB of each drive with random data from heap memory. https://web.archive.org/web/20160303200515/https://operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Destructive-Malware-Report.pdf

Lazarus Group malware SHARPKNOT overwrites and deletes the Master Boot Record (MBR) on the victim's machine and has possessed MBR wiper malware since at least 2009.  https://www.us-cert.gov/sites/default/files/publications/MAR-10135536.11.WHITE.pdf

Lazarus Group delivered RATANKBA and other malicious code to victims via a compromised legitimate website.  https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/17/b/ratankba-watering-holes-against-enterprises.html

Several Lazarus Group malware families encrypt C2 traffic using custom code that uses XOR with an ADD operation and XOR with a SUB operation. Another Lazarus Group malware sample XORs C2 traffic. Other Lazarus Group malware uses Caracachs encryption to encrypt C2 payloads. Lazarus Group has also used AES to encrypt C2 traffic.     https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf
Lazarus Group has created new LinkedIn and Twitter accounts to conduct social engineering against potential victims.   https://www.clearskysec.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Dream-Job-Campaign.pdf
Lazarus Group has created new email accounts for spearphishing operations.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/ESET_Operation_Interception.pdf

Lazarus Group malware SierraBravo-Two generates an email message via SMTP containing information about newly infected victims.  https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf

Lazarus Group has exfiltrated data and files over a C2 channel through its various tools and malware.    https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf
Lazarus Group has exfiltrated stolen data to Dropbox using a customized version of dbxcli.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/ESET_Operation_Interception.pdf
Lazarus Group has exploited Adobe Flash vulnerability CVE-2018-4878 for execution. https://securingtomorrow.mcafee.com/mcafee-labs/hidden-cobra-targets-turkish-financial-sector-new-bankshot-implant/

Lazarus Group malware SierraAlfa sends data to one of the hard-coded C2 servers chosen at random, and if the transmission fails, chooses a new C2 server to attempt the transmission again.  https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf

Several Lazarus Group has conducted word searches on compromised machines to identify specific documents of interest. Lazarus Group malware can use a common function to identify target files by their extension, and some also enumerate files and directories, including a Destover-like variant that lists files and gathers information for all drives.     https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf

Lazarus Group collected email addresses belonging to various departments of a targeted organization which were used in follow-on phishing campaigns. https://securelist.com/lazarus-threatneedle/100803/

Lazarus Group has studied publicly available information about a targeted organization to tailor spearphishing efforts against specific departments and/or individuals.   https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/ESET_Operation_Interception.pdf

Lazarus Group has targeted specific individuals within an organization with tailored job vacancy announcements.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/ESET_Operation_Interception.pdf

Lazarus Group has used a VBA Macro to set its file attributes to System and Hidden and has named files with a dot prefix to hide them from the Finder application.    https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/lazarus-resurfaces-targets-global-banks-bitcoin-users/

Lazarus Group has replaced win_fw.dll, an internal component that is executed during IDA Pro installation, with a malicious DLL to download and execute a payload. https://twitter.com/ESETresearch/status/1458438155149922312

Lazarus Group has abused the KernelCallbackTable to hijack process control flow and execute shellcode.  https://blog.malwarebytes.com/threat-intelligence/2022/01/north-koreas-lazarus-apt-leverages-windows-update-client-github-in-latest-campaign/

Lazarus Group malware TangoDelta attempts to terminate various processes associated with McAfee. Additionally, Lazarus Group malware SHARPKNOT disables the Microsoft Windows System Event Notification and Alerter services.    .https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf

Various Lazarus Group malware modifies the Windows firewall to allow incoming connections or disable it entirely using netsh.    https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf

Lazarus Group has restored malicious KernelCallbackTable code to its original state after the process execution flow has been hijacked. https://blog.malwarebytes.com/threat-intelligence/2022/01/north-koreas-lazarus-apt-leverages-windows-update-client-github-in-latest-campaign/
Lazarus Group has routinely deleted log files on a compromised router, including automatic log deletion through the use of the logrotate utility. https://securelist.com/lazarus-threatneedle/100803/

Lazarus Group malware has deleted files in various ways, including "suicide scripts" to delete malware binaries from the victim. Lazarus Group also uses secure file deletion to delete files from the victim.  https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf

Several Lazarus Group malware families use timestomping, including modifying the last write timestamp of a specified Registry key to a random date, as well as copying the timestamp for legitimate .exe files (such as calc.exe or mspaint.exe) to its dropped files.    https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf

Lazarus Group persistence mechanisms have used forfiles.exe to execute .htm files. https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2022/02/08/lolzarus-lazarus-group-incorporating-lolbins-into-campaigns

Lazarus Group has downloaded files, malware, and tools from its C2 onto a compromised host.             https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf

Lazarus Group malware KiloAlfa contains keylogging functionality.  https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf
Lazarus Group has conducted internal spearphishing from within a compromised organization. https://www.clearskysec.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Dream-Job-Campaign.pdf

Lazarus Group has disguised malicious template files as JPEG files to avoid detection. https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/operation-north-star-a-job-offer-thats-too-good-to-be-true/?hilite=%27Operation%27%2C%27North%27%2C%27Star%27

Lazarus Group has renamed system utilities such as wscript.exe and mshta.exe. https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2022/02/08/lolzarus-lazarus-group-incorporating-lolbins-into-campaigns
Lazarus Group has used a scheduled task named SRCheck to mask the execution of a malicious .dll. https://twitter.com/ESETresearch/status/1458438155149922312
Lazarus Group has renamed malicious code to disguise it as Microsoft's narrator and other legitimate files.   https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/analysis-reports/ar20-133b

Lazarus Group has used multi-stage malware components that inject later stages into separate processes. https://blog.malwarebytes.com/threat-intelligence/2022/01/north-koreas-lazarus-apt-leverages-windows-update-client-github-in-latest-campaign/

Lazarus Group has used the Windows API ObtainUserAgentString to obtain the User-Agent from a compromised host to connect to a C2 server.  Lazarus Group has also used various, often lesser known, functions to perform various types of Discovery and Process Injection.  https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/operation-north-star-a-job-offer-thats-too-good-to-be-true/?hilite=%27Operation%27%2C%27North%27%2C%27Star%27
Lazarus Group has used nmap from a router VM to scan ports on systems within the restricted segment of an enterprise network. https://securelist.com/lazarus-threatneedle/100803/

Some Lazarus Group malware uses a list of ordered port numbers to choose a port for C2 traffic, creating port-protocol mismatches.  https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf

Lazarus Group has used multiple types of encryption and encoding for their payloads, including AES, Caracachs, RC4, XOR, Base64, and other tricks such as creating aliases in code for Native API function names.           https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf
Lazarus Group has used Themida to pack malicious DLLs and other files.  https://www.clearskysec.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Dream-Job-Campaign.pdf

Lazarus Group has used a custom hashing method to resolve APIs used in shellcode. https://blog.malwarebytes.com/threat-intelligence/2022/01/north-koreas-lazarus-apt-leverages-windows-update-client-github-in-latest-campaign/

Lazarus Group has obtained a variety of tools for their operations, including Responder, PuTTy PSCP, Wake-On-Lan, ChromePass, and dbxcli.   https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/ESET_Operation_Interception.pdf
Lazarus Group has used code signing certificates issued by Sectigo RSA for some of its malware and tools. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/ESET_Operation_Interception.pdf
Lazarus Group has obtained SSL certificates for their C2 domains. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa21-048a

Lazarus Group has targeted victims with spearphishing emails containing malicious Microsoft Word documents.     https://securingtomorrow.mcafee.com/mcafee-labs/hidden-cobra-targets-turkish-financial-sector-new-bankshot-implant/
Lazarus Group has sent malicious links to victims via email.   https://securelist.com/lazarus-threatneedle/100803/
Lazarus Group has used social media platforms, including LinkedIn and Twitter, to send spearphishing messages.   https://blog.google/threat-analysis-group/new-campaign-targeting-security-researchers/

Lazarus Group malware WhiskeyAlfa-Three modifies sector 0 of the Master Boot Record (MBR) to ensure that the malware will persist even if a victim machine shuts down.  https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf

Several Lazarus Group malware families gather a list of running processes on a victim system and send it to their C2 server. A Destover-like variant used by Lazarus Group also gathers process times.      https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf
A Lazarus Group malware sample performs reflective DLL injection.  https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/lazarus-resurfaces-targets-global-banks-bitcoin-users/
Lazarus Group has used a compromised router to serve as a proxy between a victim network's corporate and restricted segments. https://securelist.com/lazarus-threatneedle/100803/
Lazarus Group has used multiple proxies to obfuscate network traffic from victims.  https://www.us-cert.gov/ncas/alerts/TA17-318A

Lazarus Group malware IndiaIndia checks Registry keys within HKCU and HKLM to determine if certain applications are present, including SecureCRT, Terminal Services, RealVNC, TightVNC, UltraVNC, Radmin, mRemote, TeamViewer, FileZilla, pcAnyware, and Remote Desktop. Another Lazarus Group malware sample checks for the presence of the following Registry key:HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Bitcoin\Bitcoin-Qt.   https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf

Lazarus Group has changed memory protection permissions then overwritten in memory DLL function code with shellcode, which was later executed via KernelCallbackTable hijacking. Lazarus Group has also used shellcode within macros to decrypt and manually map DLLs into memory at runtime.  https://blog.malwarebytes.com/threat-intelligence/2022/01/north-koreas-lazarus-apt-leverages-windows-update-client-github-in-latest-campaign/

Lazarus Group malware SierraCharlie uses RDP for propagation.  https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf

Lazarus Group malware SierraAlfa accesses the ADMIN$ share via SMB to conduct lateral movement.  https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf
Lazarus Group used SSH and the PuTTy PSCP utility to gain access to a restricted segment of a compromised network. https://securelist.com/lazarus-threatneedle/100803/

Lazarus Group has used schtasks for persistence including through the periodic execution of a remote XSL script or a dropped VBS payload.   https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/ESET_Operation_Interception.pdf
Lazarus Group has used LinkedIn to identify and target specific employees within a chosen organization.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/ESET_Operation_Interception.pdf

Lazarus Group has stopped the MSExchangeIS service to render Exchange contents inaccessible to users. https://web.archive.org/web/20160303200515/https://operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Destructive-Malware-Report.pdf
Lazarus Group has hosted malicious files on compromised as well as Lazarus Group-controlled servers.   https://www.clearskysec.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Dream-Job-Campaign.pdf

Lazarus Group has hosted custom and open-source tools on compromised as well as Lazarus Group-controlled servers. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/ESET_Operation_Interception.pdf
Lazarus Group has digitally signed malware and utilities to evade detection.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/ESET_Operation_Interception.pdf

Lazarus Group lnk files used for persistence have abused the Windows Update Client (wuauclt.exe) to execute a malicious DLL.  https://blog.malwarebytes.com/threat-intelligence/2022/01/north-koreas-lazarus-apt-leverages-windows-update-client-github-in-latest-campaign/

Lazarus Group has used mshta.exe to execute HTML pages downloaded by initial access documents.  https://blog.malwarebytes.com/threat-intelligence/2022/01/north-koreas-lazarus-apt-leverages-windows-update-client-github-in-latest-campaign/
Lazarus Group has used rgsvr32 to execute custom malware. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/ESET_Operation_Interception.pdf

Lazarus Group has used rundll32 to execute malicious payloads on a compromised host.   https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/operation-north-star-a-job-offer-thats-too-good-to-be-true/?hilite=%27Operation%27%2C%27North%27%2C%27Star%27

Several Lazarus Group malware families collect information on the type and version of the victim OS, as well as the victim computer name and CPU information. A Destover-like variant used by Lazarus Group also collects disk space information and sends it to its C2 server.      https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf

Lazarus Group has deployed malware designed not to run on computers set to Korean, Japanese, or Chinese in Windows language preferences. https://www.clearskysec.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Dream-Job-Campaign.pdf

Lazarus Group malware IndiaIndia obtains and sends to its C2 server information about the first network interface card’s configuration, including IP address, gateways, subnet mask, DHCP information, and whether WINS is available.  https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf
Lazarus Group has used net use to identify and establish a network connection with a remote host. https://securelist.com/lazarus-threatneedle/100803/

Various Lazarus Group malware enumerates logged-on users.       https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf
Lazarus Group has rebooted systems after destroying files and wiping the MBR on infected systems. https://www.us-cert.gov/sites/default/files/publications/MAR-10135536.11.WHITE.pdf

A Destover-like implant used by Lazarus Group can obtain the current system time and send it to the C2 server. https://securingtomorrow.mcafee.com/mcafee-labs/analyzing-operation-ghostsecret-attack-seeks-to-steal-data-worldwide/
Lazarus Group has used DOCX files to retrieve a malicious document template/DOTM file.  https://www.clearskysec.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Dream-Job-Campaign.pdf
Lazarus Group has sent spearphishing emails in an attempt to lure users to click on a malicious link.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/ESET_Operation_Interception.pdf

Lazarus Group has attempted to get users to launch a malicious Microsoft Word attachment delivered via a spearphishing email.     https://securingtomorrow.mcafee.com/mcafee-labs/hidden-cobra-targets-turkish-financial-sector-new-bankshot-implant/
Lazarus Group has used administrator credentials to gain access to restricted network segments. https://securelist.com/lazarus-threatneedle/100803/

Lazarus Group has used tools to detect sandbox or VMware services through identifying the presence of a debugger or related services. https://www.clearskysec.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Dream-Job-Campaign.pdf

Lazarus Group has used GitHub as C2, pulling hosted image payloads then committing command execution output to files in specific directories. https://blog.malwarebytes.com/threat-intelligence/2022/01/north-koreas-lazarus-apt-leverages-windows-update-client-github-in-latest-campaign/

Lazarus Group has used WMIC for discovery as well as to execute payloads for persistence and lateral movement.     https://web.archive.org/web/20160226161828/https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf
Lazarus Group has used WMIC to execute a remote XSL script to establish persistence. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/ESET_Operation_Interception.pdf

Lazarus Group has been observed targeting organizations using spearphishing documents with embedded malicious payloads.   Highly targeted spear phishing campaigns have been conducted against a U.S. electric grid company.  https://www.operationblockbuster.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Operation-Blockbuster-Report.pdf

Use: Magic Hound has used Powershell to discover email accounts. https://thedfirreport.com/2022/03/21/apt35-automates-initial-access-using-proxyshell

Magic Hound granted compromised email accounts read access to the email boxes of additional targeted accounts. The group then was able to authenticate to the intended victim's OWA (Outlook Web Access) portal and read hundreds of email communications for information on Middle East organizations. https://www.fireeye.com/content/dam/collateral/en/mtrends-2018.pdf

Magic Hound has registered fraudulent domains such as "mail-newyorker.com" and "news12.com.recover-session-service.site" to target specific victims with phishing attacks. https://blog.certfa.com/posts/charming-kitten-christmas-gift/
Magic Hound has acquired Amazon S3 buckets to use in C2. https://research.checkpoint.com/2022/apt35-exploits-log4j-vulnerability-to-distribute-new-modular-powershell-toolkit/

Magic Hound has conducted widespread scanning to identify public-facing systems vulnerable to Log4j (CVE-2021-44228). https://research.checkpoint.com/2022/apt35-exploits-log4j-vulnerability-to-distribute-new-modular-powershell-toolkit/
Magic Hound malware has used IRC for C2. https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/02/unit42-magic-hound-campaign-attacks-saudi-targets/
Magic Hound malware has used HTTP for C2.  https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/02/unit42-magic-hound-campaign-attacks-saudi-targets/
Magic Hound has used gzip to archive dumped LSASS process memory and RAR to stage and compress local folders.  https://www.fireeye.com/content/dam/collateral/en/mtrends-2018.pdf
Magic Hound malware has used Registry Run keys to establish persistence. https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/02/unit42-magic-hound-campaign-attacks-saudi-targets/
Magic Hound has used PowerShell for execution and privilege escalation.   https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/02/unit42-magic-hound-campaign-attacks-saudi-targets/
Magic Hound has used the command-line interface.  https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/02/unit42-magic-hound-campaign-attacks-saudi-targets/
Magic Hound malware has used VBS scripts for execution. https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/02/unit42-magic-hound-campaign-attacks-saudi-targets/

Magic Hound has compromised personal email accounts through the use of legitimate credentials and gathered additional victim information. https://securityintelligence.com/posts/new-research-exposes-iranian-threat-group-operations/
Magic Hound has used compromised domains to host links targeted to specific phishing victims.   https://www.clearskysec.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/The-Kittens-are-Back-in-Town-3.pdf

Magic Hound has created a user named DefaultAccount on compromised machines and assigned it to the Administrators and Remote Desktop Users groups. https://thedfirreport.com/2022/03/21/apt35-automates-initial-access-using-proxyshell

Magic Hound has used a web shell to exfiltrate a ZIP file containing a dump of LSASS memory on a compromised machine. https://thedfirreport.com/2022/03/21/apt35-automates-initial-access-using-proxyshell
Magic Hound has conducted watering-hole attacks through media and magazine websites. https://www.clearskysec.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/The-Kittens-are-Back-in-Town-3.pdf
Magic Hound has compromised email credentials in order to steal sensitive data. https://blog.certfa.com/posts/charming-kitten-christmas-gift/
Magic Hound has collected .PST archives. https://www.fireeye.com/content/dam/collateral/en/mtrends-2018.pdf
Magic Hound has exported emails from compromised Exchange servers. https://thedfirreport.com/2022/03/21/apt35-automates-initial-access-using-proxyshell

Magic Hound has created fake LinkedIn and other social media accounts to contact targets and convince them--through messages and voice communications--to open malicious links. https://www.clearskysec.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/The-Kittens-are-Back-in-Town-3.pdf
Magic Hound has established email accounts using fake personas for spearphishing operations.  https://securityintelligence.com/posts/new-research-exposes-iranian-threat-group-operations/

Magic Hound has used open-source JNDI exploit kits to exploit Log4j (CVE-2021-44228) and has exploited ProxyShell (CVE-2021-34473, CVE-2021-34523, CVE-2021-31207) on MS Exchange servers.   https://research.checkpoint.com/2022/apt35-exploits-log4j-vulnerability-to-distribute-new-modular-powershell-toolkit/

Magic Hound malware can list a victim's logical drives and the type, as well the total/free space of the fixed devices. Other malware can list a directory's contents. https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/02/unit42-magic-hound-campaign-attacks-saudi-targets/

Magic Hound has acquired mobile phone numbers of potential targets, possibly for mobile malware or additional phishing operations. https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/operation-spoofedscholars-conversation-ta453

Magic Hound gathered credentials from two victims that they then attempted to validate across 75 different websites. https://securityintelligence.com/posts/new-research-exposes-iranian-threat-group-operations/
Magic Hound has acquired the personal email addresses of some individuals they intend to target. https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/operation-spoofedscholars-conversation-ta453

Magic Hound malware has a function to determine whether the C2 server wishes to execute the newly dropped file in a hidden window. https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/02/unit42-magic-hound-campaign-attacks-saudi-targets/

Magic Hound has disabled LSA protection on compromised hosts using "reg" add HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\LSA /v RunAsPPL /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f. https://thedfirreport.com/2022/03/21/apt35-automates-initial-access-using-proxyshell
Magic Hound has disabled antivirus services on targeted systems in order to upload malicious payloads. https://thedfirreport.com/2022/03/21/apt35-automates-initial-access-using-proxyshell

Magic Hound has added the following rule to a victim's Windows firewall to allow RDP traffic - "netsh" advfirewall firewall add rule name="Terminal Server" dir=in action=allow protocol=TCP localport=3389. https://thedfirreport.com/2022/03/21/apt35-automates-initial-access-using-proxyshell
Magic Hound has removed mailbox export requests from compromised Exchange servers. https://thedfirreport.com/2022/03/21/apt35-automates-initial-access-using-proxyshell
Magic Hound has deleted and overwrote files to cover tracks.  https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/02/unit42-magic-hound-campaign-attacks-saudi-targets/
Magic Hound has downloaded additional code and files from servers onto victims.  https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/02/unit42-magic-hound-campaign-attacks-saudi-targets/
Magic Hound malware is capable of keylogging. https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/02/unit42-magic-hound-campaign-attacks-saudi-targets/
Magic Hound has used the name dllhost.exe to mask a malicious tool used in C2. https://thedfirreport.com/2022/03/21/apt35-automates-initial-access-using-proxyshell
Magic Hound has modified Registry settings for security tools. https://thedfirreport.com/2022/03/21/apt35-automates-initial-access-using-proxyshell
Magic Hound malware has communicated with its C2 server over TCP port 4443 using HTTP. https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/02/unit42-magic-hound-campaign-attacks-saudi-targets/

Magic Hound malware has used base64-encoded commands and files, and has also encrypted embedded strings with AES. https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/02/unit42-magic-hound-campaign-attacks-saudi-targets/
Magic Hound has obtained and used open-source penetration testing tools like Havij, sqlmap, Metasploit, and Mimikatz.   https://blog.checkpoint.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/11/rocket-kitten-report.pdf

Magic Hound has stolen domain credentials by dumping LSASS process memory with comsvcs.dll and from a Microsoft Active Directory Domain Controller using Mimikatz.  https://www.fireeye.com/content/dam/collateral/en/mtrends-2018.pdf

Magic Hound has sent malicious URL links through email to victims. In some cases the URLs were shortened or linked to Word documents with malicious macros that executed PowerShells scripts to download Pupy.   https://www.secureworks.com/blog/iranian-pupyrat-bites-middle-eastern-organizations

Magic Hound used various social media channels (such as LinkedIn) as well as messaging services (such as WhatsApp) to spearphish victims.   https://www.secureworks.com/research/the-curious-case-of-mia-ash
Magic Hound has used SMS and email messages with links designed to steal credentials.    https://blog.certfa.com/posts/charming-kitten-christmas-gift/
Magic Hound malware can list running processes. https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/02/unit42-magic-hound-campaign-attacks-saudi-targets/
Magic Hound has used Remote Desktop Services on targeted systems. https://thedfirreport.com/2022/03/21/apt35-automates-initial-access-using-proxyshell
Magic Hound has used scheduled tasks to establish persistence. https://thedfirreport.com/2022/03/21/apt35-automates-initial-access-using-proxyshell
Magic Hound malware can take a screenshot and upload the file to its C2 server. https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/02/unit42-magic-hound-campaign-attacks-saudi-targets/
Magic Hound has used multiple web shells to gain execution. https://thedfirreport.com/2022/03/21/apt35-automates-initial-access-using-proxyshell
Magic Hound has used rundll32.exe to execute MiniDump from comsvcs.dll when dumping LSASS memory. https://thedfirreport.com/2022/03/21/apt35-automates-initial-access-using-proxyshell

Magic Hound malware has used a PowerShell command to check the victim system architecture to determine if it is an x64 machine. Other malware has obtained the OS version, UUID, and computer/host name to send to the C2 server.  https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/02/unit42-magic-hound-campaign-attacks-saudi-targets/

Magic Hound malware gathers the victim's local IP address, MAC address, and external IP address.  https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/02/unit42-magic-hound-campaign-attacks-saudi-targets/
Magic Hound has used quser.exe to identify existing RDP connections. https://thedfirreport.com/2022/03/21/apt35-automates-initial-access-using-proxyshell
Magic Hound malware has obtained the victim username and sent it to the C2 server.  https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/02/unit42-magic-hound-campaign-attacks-saudi-targets/
Magic Hound has attempted to lure victims into opening malicious links embedded in emails.  https://www.clearskysec.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/The-Kittens-are-Back-in-Town-3.pdf
Magic Hound has attempted to lure victims into opening malicious email attachments. https://www.clearskysec.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/The-Kittens-are-Back-in-Town-3.pdf
Magic Hound malware can use a SOAP Web service to communicate with its C2 server. https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/02/unit42-magic-hound-campaign-attacks-saudi-targets/
Magic Hound has used a tool to run cmd /c wmic computersystem get domain for discovery. https://thedfirreport.com/2022/03/21/apt35-automates-initial-access-using-proxyshell

menuPass has collected various files from the compromised computers.  https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/two-chinese-hackers-associated-ministry-state-security-charged-global-computer-intrusion

menuPass stages data prior to exfiltration in multi-part archives, often saved in the Recycle Bin. https://web.archive.org/web/20220224041316/https:/www.pwc.co.uk/cyber-security/pdf/cloud-hopper-report-final-v4.pdf

menuPass has staged data on remote MSP systems or other victim networks prior to exfiltration.  https://web.archive.org/web/20220224041316/https:/www.pwc.co.uk/cyber-security/pdf/cloud-hopper-report-final-v4.pdf

menuPass has used certutil in a macro to decode base64-encoded content contained in a dropper document attached to an email. menuPass has used dynamic DNS service providers to host malicious domains. https://www.justice.gov/opa/page/file/1122671/download
menuPass has leveraged vulnerabilities in Pulse Secure VPNs to hijack sessions. https://securelist.com/apt10-sophisticated-multi-layered-loader-ecipekac-discovered-in-a41apt-campaign/101519/
menuPass has used tools to exploit the ZeroLogon vulnerability (CVE-2020-1472). https://symantec-enterprise-blogs.security.com/blogs/threat-intelligence/cicada-apt10-japan-espionage

menuPass has searched compromised systems for folders of interest including those related to HR, audit and expense, and meeting memos. https://symantec-enterprise-blogs.security.com/blogs/threat-intelligence/cicada-apt10-japan-espionage
menuPass has used DLL search order hijacking. https://web.archive.org/web/20220224041316/https:/www.pwc.co.uk/cyber-security/pdf/cloud-hopper-report-final-v4.pdf
menuPass has used DLL side-loading to launch versions of Mimikatz and PwDump6 as well as UPPERCUT.   https://www.pwc.co.uk/cyber-security/pdf/cloud-hopper-annex-b-final.pdf
menuPass has used Wevtutil to remove PowerShell execution logs. https://securelist.com/apt10-sophisticated-multi-layered-loader-ecipekac-discovered-in-a41apt-campaign/101519/
A menuPass macro deletes files after it has decoded and decompressed them.  https://www.accenture.com/t20180423T055005Z_w_/se-en/_acnmedia/PDF-76/Accenture-Hogfish-Threat-Analysis.pdf
menuPass has installed updates and new malware on victims.  https://web.archive.org/web/20220224041316/https:/www.pwc.co.uk/cyber-security/pdf/cloud-hopper-report-final-v4.pdf
menuPass has used key loggers to steal usernames and passwords. https://www.justice.gov/opa/page/file/1122671/download

menuPass has used esentutl to change file extensions to their true type that were masquerading as .txt files. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2018/09/apt10-targeting-japanese-corporations-using-updated-ttps.html

menuPass has renamed certutil and moved it to a different location on the system to avoid detection based on use of the tool. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2018/09/apt10-targeting-japanese-corporations-using-updated-ttps.html
menuPass has been seen changing malicious files to appear legitimate. https://www.justice.gov/opa/page/file/1122671/download
menuPass has used native APIs including GetModuleFileName, lstrcat, CreateFile, and ReadFile. https://symantec-enterprise-blogs.security.com/blogs/threat-intelligence/cicada-apt10-japan-espionage
menuPass has used tcping.exe, similar to Ping, to probe port status on systems of interest. https://www.pwc.co.uk/cyber-security/pdf/cloud-hopper-annex-b-final.pdf

menuPass has encoded strings in its malware with base64 as well as with a simple, single-byte XOR obfuscation using key 0x40.   https://www.accenture.com/t20180423T055005Z_w_/se-en/_acnmedia/PDF-76/Accenture-Hogfish-Threat-Analysis.pdf
menuPass has used and modified open-source tools like Impacket, Mimikatz, and pwdump. https://www.pwc.co.uk/cyber-security/pdf/cloud-hopper-annex-b-final.pdf
menuPass has used a modified version of pentesting tools wmiexec.vbs and secretsdump.py to dump credentials.  https://www.pwc.co.uk/cyber-security/pdf/cloud-hopper-annex-b-final.pdf
menuPass has used Ntdsutil to dump credentials. https://symantec-enterprise-blogs.security.com/blogs/threat-intelligence/cicada-apt10-japan-espionage
menuPass has used a modified version of pentesting tools wmiexec.vbs and secretsdump.py to dump credentials.  https://www.pwc.co.uk/cyber-security/pdf/cloud-hopper-annex-b-final.pdf

menuPass has sent malicious Office documents via email as part of spearphishing campaigns as well as executables disguised as documents.    https://www.pwc.co.uk/cyber-security/pdf/cloud-hopper-annex-b-final.pdf
menuPass has used process hollowing in iexplore.exe to load the RedLeaves implant. https://www.accenture.com/t20180423T055005Z_w_/se-en/_acnmedia/PDF-76/Accenture-Hogfish-Threat-Analysis.pdf
menuPass has used a global service provider's IP as a proxy for C2 traffic from a victim.  https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2017/04/apt10_menupass_grou.html
menuPass has used RDP connections to move across the victim network.  https://web.archive.org/web/20220224041316/https:/www.pwc.co.uk/cyber-security/pdf/cloud-hopper-report-final-v4.pdf
menuPass has used Putty Secure Copy Client (PSCP) to transfer data. https://web.archive.org/web/20220224041316/https:/www.pwc.co.uk/cyber-security/pdf/cloud-hopper-report-final-v4.pdf

menuPass uses scripts to enumerate IP ranges on the victim network. menuPass has also issued the command net view /domain to a PlugX implant to gather information about remote systems on the network.  https://www.pwc.co.uk/cyber-security/pdf/cloud-hopper-annex-b-final.pdf
menuPass has used a script (atexec.py) to execute a command on a target machine via Task Scheduler. https://www.pwc.co.uk/cyber-security/pdf/cloud-hopper-annex-b-final.pdf

menuPass has resized and added data to the certificate table to enable the signing of modified files with legitimate signatures. https://securelist.com/apt10-sophisticated-multi-layered-loader-ecipekac-discovered-in-a41apt-campaign/101519/
menuPass has used InstallUtil.exe to execute malicious software. https://www.pwc.co.uk/cyber-security/pdf/cloud-hopper-annex-b-final.pdf
menuPass has used several tools to scan for open NetBIOS nameservers and enumerate NetBIOS sessions. https://www.pwc.co.uk/cyber-security/pdf/cloud-hopper-annex-b-final.pdf
menuPass has used net use to conduct connectivity checks to machines. https://web.archive.org/web/20220224041316/https:/www.pwc.co.uk/cyber-security/pdf/cloud-hopper-report-final-v4.pdf
menuPass has used legitimate access granted to Managed Service Providers in order to access victims of interest.     https://www.pwc.co.uk/cyber-security/pdf/cloud-hopper-annex-b-final.pdf

menuPass has attempted to get victims to open malicious files such as Windows Shortcuts (.lnk) and/or Microsoft Office documents, sent via email as part of spearphishing campaigns.     https://www.pwc.co.uk/cyber-security/pdf/cloud-hopper-annex-b-final.pdf

menuPass has used valid accounts including shared between Managed Service Providers and clients to move between the two environments.    https://web.archive.org/web/20220224041316/https:/www.pwc.co.uk/cyber-security/pdf/cloud-hopper-report-final-v4.pdf
menuPass has used a modified version of pentesting script wmiexec.vbs, which logs into a remote machine using WMI.   https://www.pwc.co.uk/cyber-security/pdf/cloud-hopper-annex-b-final.pdf

Use: TeamTNT has added RSA keys in authorized_keys.  https://blog.aquasec.com/container-security-tnt-container-attack
TeamTNT has obtained domains to host their payloads. https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/black-t-cryptojacking-variant/
TeamTNT has scanned specific lists of target IP addresses. https://documents.trendmicro.com/assets/white_papers/wp-tracking-the-activities-of-teamTNT.pdf

TeamTNT has scanned for vulnerabilities in IoT devices and other related resources such as the Docker API. https://documents.trendmicro.com/assets/white_papers/wp-tracking-the-activities-of-teamTNT.pdf
TeamTNT has used an IRC bot for C2 communications. https://documents.trendmicro.com/assets/white_papers/wp-tracking-the-activities-of-teamTNT.pdf

TeamTNT has the curl command to send credentials over HTTP and the curl and wget commands to download new software.    TeamTNT has also used a custom user agent HTTP header in shell scripts. https://www.intezer.com/blog/cloud-security/attackers-abusing-legitimate-cloud-monitoring-tools-to-conduct-cyber-attacks/
TeamTNT has added batch scripts to the startup folder. https://cybersecurity.att.com/blogs/labs-research/teamtnt-with-new-campaign-aka-chimaera
TeamTNT has executed PowerShell commands in batch scripts. https://cybersecurity.att.com/blogs/labs-research/teamtnt-with-new-campaign-aka-chimaera
TeamTNT has used batch scripts to download tools and executing cryptocurrency miners. https://cybersecurity.att.com/blogs/labs-research/teamtnt-with-new-campaign-aka-chimaera
TeamTNT has used shell scripts for execution.  https://documents.trendmicro.com/assets/white_papers/wp-tracking-the-activities-of-teamTNT.pdf
TeamTNT executed Hildegard through the kubelet API run command and by executing commands on running containers. https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hildegard-malware-teamtnt/

TeamTNT has checked for running containers with docker ps and for specific container names with docker inspect.  TeamTNT has also searched for Kubernetes pods running in a local network. https://documents.trendmicro.com/assets/white_papers/wp-tracking-the-activities-of-teamTNT.pdf
TeamTNT has created local privileged users on victim machines. https://www.intezer.com/blog/cloud-security/attackers-abusing-legitimate-cloud-monitoring-tools-to-conduct-cyber-attacks/

TeamTNT has established persistence through the creation of a cryptocurrency mining system service using systemctl.  https://documents.trendmicro.com/assets/white_papers/wp-tracking-the-activities-of-teamTNT.pdf
TeamTNT has used malware that adds cryptocurrency miners as a service. https://cybersecurity.att.com/blogs/labs-research/teamtnt-with-new-campaign-aka-chimaera
TeamTNT has aggregated collected credentials in text files before exfiltrating. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/2022/04/teamtnt-targeting-aws-alibaba.html
TeamTNT has used a script that decodes a Base64-encoded version of WeaveWorks Scope. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/2022/04/teamtnt-targeting-aws-alibaba.html

TeamTNT has deployed different types of containers into victim environments to facilitate execution.   TeamTNT has also transferred cryptocurrency mining software to Kubernetes clusters discovered within local IP address ranges. https://www.intezer.com/blog/cloud-security/attackers-abusing-legitimate-cloud-monitoring-tools-to-conduct-cyber-attacks/
TeamTNT has developed custom malware such as Hildegard. https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hildegard-malware-teamtnt/

TeamTNT has deployed privileged containers that mount the filesystem of victim machine.  https://www.intezer.com/blog/cloud-security/attackers-abusing-legitimate-cloud-monitoring-tools-to-conduct-cyber-attacks/
TeamTNT has sent locally staged files with collected credentials to C2 servers using cURL. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/2022/04/teamtnt-targeting-aws-alibaba.html

TeamTNT has used open-source tools such as Weave Scope to target exposed Docker API ports and gain initial access to victim environments.   TeamTNT has also targeted exposed kubelets for Kubernetes environments. https://www.intezer.com/blog/cloud-security/attackers-abusing-legitimate-cloud-monitoring-tools-to-conduct-cyber-attacks/
TeamTNT has used a script that checks /proc/*/environ for environment variables related to AWS. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/2022/04/teamtnt-targeting-aws-alibaba.html
TeamTNT has modified the permissions on binaries with chattr.  https://documents.trendmicro.com/assets/white_papers/wp-tracking-the-activities-of-teamTNT.pdf

TeamTNT has disabled and uninstalled security tools such as Alibaba, Tencent, and BMC cloud monitoring agents on cloud-based infrastructure.  https://cybersecurity.att.com/blogs/labs-research/teamtnt-with-new-campaign-aka-chimaera
TeamTNT has disabled iptables. https://blog.aquasec.com/container-security-tnt-container-attack
TeamTNT has removed system logs from /var/log/syslog. https://blog.aquasec.com/container-security-tnt-container-attack
TeamTNT has cleared command history with history -c.  https://documents.trendmicro.com/assets/white_papers/wp-tracking-the-activities-of-teamTNT.pdf

TeamTNT has used a payload that removes itself after running. TeamTNT also has deleted locally staged files for collecting credentials or scan results for local IP addresses after exfiltrating them.  https://cybersecurity.att.com/blogs/labs-research/teamtnt-with-new-campaign-aka-chimaera

TeamTNT has the curl and wget commands as well as batch scripts to download new tools.  https://www.intezer.com/blog/cloud-security/attackers-abusing-legitimate-cloud-monitoring-tools-to-conduct-cyber-attacks/
TeamTNT has disguised their scripts with docker-related file names. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/2022/04/teamtnt-targeting-aws-alibaba.html
TeamTNT has replaced .dockerd and .dockerenv with their own scripts and cryptocurrency mining software. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/2022/04/teamtnt-targeting-aws-alibaba.html

TeamTNT has used masscan to search for open Docker API ports and Kubernetes clusters.    TeamTNT has also used malware that utilizes zmap and zgrab to search for vulnerable services in cloud environments. https://www.cadosecurity.com/team-tnt-the-first-crypto-mining-worm-to-steal-aws-credentials/
TeamTNT has encrypted its binaries via AES and encoded files using Base64.  https://documents.trendmicro.com/assets/white_papers/wp-tracking-the-activities-of-teamTNT.pdf
TeamTNT has used UPX and Ezuri packer to pack its binaries. https://documents.trendmicro.com/assets/white_papers/wp-tracking-the-activities-of-teamTNT.pdf
TeamTNT has searched for attached VGA devices using lspci. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/2022/04/teamtnt-targeting-aws-alibaba.html

TeamTNT has searched for rival malware and removes it if found.  TeamTNT has also searched for running processes containing the strings aliyun or liyun to identify machines running Alibaba Cloud Security tools. https://documents.trendmicro.com/assets/white_papers/wp-tracking-the-activities-of-teamTNT.pdf
TeamTNT has established tmate sessions for C2 communications.  https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hildegard-malware-teamtnt/

TeamTNT has used SSH to connect back to victim machines.  TeamTNT has also used SSH to transfer tools and payloads onto victim hosts and execute them. https://www.intezer.com/blog/cloud-security/attackers-abusing-legitimate-cloud-monitoring-tools-to-conduct-cyber-attacks/

TeamTNT has deployed XMRig Docker images to mine cryptocurrency.   TeamTNT has also infected Docker containers and Kubernetes clusters with XMRig, and used RainbowMiner and lolMiner for mining cryptocurrency. https://www.lacework.com/blog/taking-teamtnt-docker-images-offline/

TeamTNT has used rootkits such as the open-source Diamorphine rootkit and their custom bots to hide cryptocurrency mining activities on the machine.   https://documents.trendmicro.com/assets/white_papers/wp-tracking-the-activities-of-teamTNT.pdf
TeamTNT has searched for security products on infected machines.  https://cybersecurity.att.com/blogs/labs-research/teamtnt-with-new-campaign-aka-chimaera
TeamTNT has uploaded backdoored Docker images to Docker Hub. https://www.lacework.com/blog/taking-teamtnt-docker-images-offline/

TeamTNT has searched for system version, architecture, disk partition, logical volume, and hostname information.  https://cybersecurity.att.com/blogs/labs-research/teamtnt-with-new-campaign-aka-chimaera
TeamTNT has enumerated the host machine’s IP address. https://documents.trendmicro.com/assets/white_papers/wp-tracking-the-activities-of-teamTNT.pdf

TeamTNT has run netstat -anp to search for rival malware connections.  TeamTNT has also used libprocesshider to modify /etc/ld.so.preload. https://documents.trendmicro.com/assets/white_papers/wp-tracking-the-activities-of-teamTNT.pdf

Transparent Tribe has crafted VBS-based malicious documents.  
For C0011, Transparent Tribe used malicious VBA macros within a lure document as part of the Crimson malware installation process onto a compromised host. https://www.proofpoint.com/sites/default/files/proofpoint-operation-transparent-tribe-threat-insight-en.pdf
Transparent Tribe has compromised domains for use in targeted malicious campaigns. https://www.proofpoint.com/sites/default/files/proofpoint-operation-transparent-tribe-threat-insight-en.pdf
For C0011, Transparent Tribe established SSL certificates on the typo-squatted domains the group registered. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/2022/07/transparent-tribe-targets-education.html

Transparent Tribe has used websites with malicious hyperlinks and iframes to infect targeted victims with Crimson, njRAT, and other malicious tools.   https://www.proofpoint.com/sites/default/files/proofpoint-operation-transparent-tribe-threat-insight-en.pdf
Transparent Tribe has used dynamic DNS services to set up C2. https://www.proofpoint.com/sites/default/files/proofpoint-operation-transparent-tribe-threat-insight-en.pdf

Transparent Tribe has crafted malicious files to exploit CVE-2012-0158 and CVE-2010-3333 for execution. https://www.proofpoint.com/sites/default/files/proofpoint-operation-transparent-tribe-threat-insight-en.pdf
Transparent Tribe can hide legitimate directories and replace them with malicious copies of the same name. https://securelist.com/transparent-tribe-part-1/98127/
Transparent Tribe can mimic legitimate Windows directories by using the same icons and names. https://securelist.com/transparent-tribe-part-1/98127/
Transparent Tribe has dropped encoded executables on compromised hosts. https://www.proofpoint.com/sites/default/files/proofpoint-operation-transparent-tribe-threat-insight-en.pdf

Transparent Tribe has sent spearphishing e-mails with attachments to deliver malicious payloads.     
During C0011, Transparent Tribe sent malicious attachments via email to student targets in India. https://www.proofpoint.com/sites/default/files/proofpoint-operation-transparent-tribe-threat-insight-en.pdf

Transparent Tribe has embedded links to malicious downloads in e-mails.  
During C0011, Transparent Tribe sent emails containing a malicious link to student targets in India. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/2021/02/obliquerat-new-campaign.html
For C0011, Transparent Tribe hosted malicious documents on domains registered by the group. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/2022/07/transparent-tribe-targets-education.html

Transparent Tribe has directed users to open URLs hosting malicious content.  
During C0011, Transparent Tribe relied on student targets to click on a malicious link sent via email. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/2021/02/obliquerat-new-campaign.html

Transparent Tribe has used weaponized documents in e-mail to compromise targeted systems.     
During C0011, Transparent Tribe relied on a student target to open a malicious document delivered via email. https://www.proofpoint.com/sites/default/files/proofpoint-operation-transparent-tribe-threat-insight-en.pdf

Use: Turla RPC backdoors can impersonate or steal process tokens before executing commands. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2019/05/29/turla-powershell-usage/
Turla has used net user to enumerate local accounts on the system.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/ESET_Turla_ComRAT.pdf
Turla has used net user /domain to enumerate domain accounts. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/ESET_Turla_ComRAT.pdf
Turla has created web accounts including Dropbox and GitHub for C2 and document exfiltration. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2020/12/02/turla-crutch-keeping-back-door-open/
Turla has used HTTP and HTTPS for C2 communications.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/ESET_Turla_Mosquito.pdf
Turla has used multiple backdoors which communicate with a C2 server via email attachments. https://go.crowdstrike.com/rs/281-OBQ-266/images/Report2020CrowdStrikeGlobalThreatReport.pdf
Turla has encrypted files stolen from connected USB drives into a RAR file before exfiltration. https://www.symantec.com/blogs/threat-intelligence/waterbug-espionage-governments

A Turla Javascript backdoor added a local_update_check value under the Registry key HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run to establish persistence. Additionally, a Turla custom executable containing Metasploit shellcode is saved to the Startup folder to gain persistence.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/ESET_Turla_Mosquito.pdf

Turla established persistence by adding a Shell value under the Registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/ESET_Turla_Mosquito.pdf
Turla may attempt to connect to systems within a victim's network using net use commands and a predefined list or collection of passwords. https://securelist.com/the-epic-turla-operation/65545/

Turla has used PowerShell to execute commands/scripts, in some cases via a custom executable or code from Empire's PSInject.    Turla has also used PowerShell scripts to load and execute malware in memory.https://www.welivesecurity.com/2018/05/22/turla-mosquito-shift-towards-generic-tools/
Turla RPC backdoors have used cmd.exe to execute commands.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/2019/05/29/turla-powershell-usage/
Turla has used VBS scripts throughout its operations. https://www.symantec.com/blogs/threat-intelligence/waterbug-espionage-governments
Turla has used IronPython scripts as part of the IronNetInjector toolchain to drop payloads. https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/ironnetinjector/
Turla has used various JavaScript-based backdoors. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/ESET_Turla_Mosquito.pdf
Turla has used the VPS infrastructure of compromised Iranian threat actors. https://media.defense.gov/2019/Oct/18/2002197242/-1/-1/0/NSA_CSA_Turla_20191021%20ver%204%20-%20nsa.gov.pdf
Turla has used compromised servers as infrastructure.   https://www.recordedfuture.com/turla-apt-infrastructure/
Turla has frequently used compromised WordPress sites for C2 infrastructure. https://www.recordedfuture.com/turla-apt-infrastructure/
Turla has gathered credentials from the Windows Credential Manager tool. https://www.symantec.com/blogs/threat-intelligence/waterbug-espionage-governments
Turla has used a custom .NET tool to collect documents from an organization's internal central database. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/ESET_Turla_ComRAT.pdf
Turla RPC backdoors can upload files from victim machines. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2019/05/29/turla-powershell-usage/
Turla RPC backdoors can collect files from USB thumb drives.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/2019/05/29/turla-powershell-usage/

Turla has used a custom decryption routine, which pulls key and salt values from other artifacts such as a WMI filter or PowerShell Profile, to decode encrypted PowerShell payloads. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2019/05/29/turla-powershell-usage/
Turla has developed its own unique malware for use in operations. https://www.recordedfuture.com/turla-apt-infrastructure/
Turla has infected victims using watering holes.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/ESET_Turla_ComRAT.pdf
Turla has used WMI event filters and consumers to establish persistence. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2019/05/29/turla-powershell-usage/
Turla has used PowerShell profiles to maintain persistence on an infected machine. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2019/05/29/turla-powershell-usage/

Turla has used WebDAV to upload stolen USB files to a cloud drive.  Turla has also exfiltrated stolen files to OneDrive and 4shared. https://www.symantec.com/blogs/threat-intelligence/waterbug-espionage-governments
Turla has exploited vulnerabilities in the VBoxDrv.sys driver to obtain kernel mode privileges. https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/acidbox-rare-malware/

Turla surveys a system upon check-in to discover files in specific locations on the hard disk %TEMP% directory, the current user's desktop, the Program Files directory, and Recent.   Turla RPC backdoors have also searched for files matching the lPH*.dll pattern. https://securelist.com/the-epic-turla-operation/65545/
Turla surveys a system upon check-in to discover Group Policy details using the gpresult command. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/ESET_Turla_ComRAT.pdf
Turla has used a AMSI bypass, which patches the in-memory amsi.dll, in PowerShell scripts to bypass Windows antimalware products. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2019/05/29/turla-powershell-usage/
Turla has used shellcode to download Meterpreter after compromising a victim. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2018/05/22/turla-mosquito-shift-towards-generic-tools/
Turla RPC backdoors can be used to transfer files to/from victim machines on the local network.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/2019/05/29/turla-powershell-usage/
Turla has used the Registry to store encrypted payloads.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/2019/05/29/turla-powershell-usage/

Turla and its RPC backdoors have used APIs calls for various tasks related to subverting AMSI and accessing then executing commands through RPC and/or named pipes. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2019/05/29/turla-powershell-usage/

Turla has used encryption (including salted 3DES via PowerSploit's Out-EncryptedScript.ps1), random variable names, and base64 encoding to obfuscate PowerShell commands and payloads. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2019/05/29/turla-powershell-usage/

Based on comparison of Gazer versions, Turla made an effort to obfuscate strings in the malware that could be used as IoCs, including the mutex name and named pipe. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/eset-gazer.pdf
Turla has used malware obtained after compromising other threat actors, such as OilRig.  https://media.defense.gov/2019/Oct/18/2002197242/-1/-1/0/NSA_CSA_Turla_20191021%20ver%204%20-%20nsa.gov.pdf
Turla has obtained and customized publicly-available tools like Mimikatz. https://www.symantec.com/blogs/threat-intelligence/waterbug-espionage-governments
Turla has used net accounts and net accounts /domain to acquire password policy information. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/ESET_Turla_ComRAT.pdf
Turla has used fsutil fsinfo drives to list connected drives. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/ESET_Turla_ComRAT.pdf

Turla has used net localgroup and net localgroup Administrators to enumerate group information, including members of the local administrators group. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/ESET_Turla_ComRAT.pdf
Turla has used net group "Domain Admins" /domain to identify domain administrators. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/ESET_Turla_ComRAT.pdf

Turla attempted to trick targets into clicking on a link featuring a seemingly legitimate domain from Adobe.com to download their malware and gain initial access. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/ESET_Turla_Mosquito.pdf

Turla surveys a system upon check-in to discover running processes using the tasklist /v command.  Turla RPC backdoors have also enumerated processes associated with specific open ports or named pipes. https://securelist.com/the-epic-turla-operation/65545/

Turla has also used PowerSploit's Invoke-ReflectivePEInjection.ps1 to reflectively load a PowerShell payload into a random process on the victim system. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2019/05/29/turla-powershell-usage/
Turla has used Metasploit to perform reflective DLL injection in order to escalate privileges.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/2018/05/22/turla-mosquito-shift-towards-generic-tools/
Turla RPC backdoors have included local UPnP RPC proxies. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2019/05/29/turla-powershell-usage/
Turla has compromised internal network systems to act as a proxy to forward traffic to C2. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/2021/09/tinyturla.html

Turla surveys a system upon check-in to discover information in the Windows Registry with the reg query command.  Turla has also retrieved PowerShell payloads hidden in Registry keys as well as checking keys associated with null session named pipes . https://securelist.com/the-epic-turla-operation/65545/
Turla used net use commands to connect to lateral systems within a network. https://securelist.com/the-epic-turla-operation/65545/

Turla surveys a system upon check-in to discover remote systems on a local network using the net view and net view /DOMAIN commands. Turla has also used net group "Domain Computers" /domain, net group "Domain Controllers" /domain, and net group "Exchange Servers" /domain to enumerate domain computers, including the organization's DC and Exchange Server.  https://securelist.com/the-epic-turla-operation/65545/

Turla has obtained information on security software, including security logging information that may indicate whether their malware has been detected. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/ESET_Turla_ComRAT.pdf

Turla has modified variables in kernel memory to turn off Driver Signature Enforcement after exploiting vulnerabilities that obtained kernel mode privileges.  https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/acidbox-rare-malware/
Turla surveys a system upon check-in to discover operating system configuration details using the systeminfo and set commands.  https://securelist.com/the-epic-turla-operation/65545/

Turla surveys a system upon check-in to discover network configuration details using the arp -a, nbtstat -n, net config, ipconfig /all, and route commands, as well as NBTscan.    Turla RPC backdoors have also retrieved registered RPC interface information from process memory. https://securelist.com/the-epic-turla-operation/65545/
Turla has used tracert to check internet connectivity. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/ESET_Turla_ComRAT.pdf

Turla surveys a system upon check-in to discover active local network connections using the netstat -an, net use, net file, and net session commands.   Turla RPC backdoors have also enumerated the IPv4 TCP connection table via the GetTcpTable2 API call. https://securelist.com/the-epic-turla-operation/65545/
Turla surveys a system upon check-in to discover running services and associated processes using the tasklist /svc command. https://securelist.com/the-epic-turla-operation/65545/
Turla surveys a system upon check-in to discover the system time by using the net time command. https://securelist.com/the-epic-turla-operation/65545/
Turla has used spearphishing via a link to get users to download and run their malware. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/ESET_Turla_Mosquito.pdf
Turla has abused local accounts that have the same password across the victim’s network. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2020/12/02/turla-crutch-keeping-back-door-open/

Turla has used legitimate web services including Pastebin, Dropbox, and GitHub for C2 communications.  https://www.accenture.com/us-en/blogs/cyber-defense/turla-belugasturgeon-compromises-government-entity
A Turla JavaScript backdoor has used Google Apps Script as its C2 server.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/ESET_Turla_Mosquito.pdf

Use: Wizard Spider has identified domain admins through the use of "net group ‘Domain admins’" commands. https://thedfirreport.com/2020/10/08/ryuks-return/

Wizard Spider has used the Invoke-Inveigh PowerShell cmdlets, likely for name service poisoning. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2020/10/kegtap-and-singlemalt-with-a-ransomware-chaser.html
Wizard Spider has used HTTP for network communications. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/timelining-grim-spiders-big-game-hunting-tactics/

Wizard Spider has established persistence via the Registry key HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run and a shortcut within the startup folder.  https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-302a

Wizard Spider has established persistence using Userinit by adding the Registry key HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2020/10/kegtap-and-singlemalt-with-a-ransomware-chaser.html

Wizard Spider has used macros to execute PowerShell scripts to download malware on victim's machines.  It has also used PowerShell to execute commands and move laterally through a victim network.   https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/timelining-grim-spiders-big-game-hunting-tactics/
Wizard Spider has used cmd.exe to execute commands on a victim's machine. https://thedfirreport.com/2020/10/08/ryuks-return/
Wizard Spider has installed TrickBot as a service named ControlServiceA in order to establish persistence. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/timelining-grim-spiders-big-game-hunting-tactics/

Wizard Spider has collected and staged credentials and network enumeration information, using the networkdll and psfin TrickBot modules. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/timelining-grim-spiders-big-game-hunting-tactics/
Wizard Spider has exfiltrated victim information using FTP.  https://thedfirreport.com/2020/10/08/ryuks-return/

Wizard Spider has exfiltrated domain credentials and network enumeration information over command and control (C2) channels. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/timelining-grim-spiders-big-game-hunting-tactics/

Wizard Spider has exploited or attempted to exploit Zerologon (CVE-2020-1472) and EternalBlue (MS17-010) vulnerabilities.   https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2020/10/kegtap-and-singlemalt-with-a-ransomware-chaser.html

Wizard Spider has accessed victim networks by using stolen credentials to access the corporate VPN infrastructure. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2020/10/kegtap-and-singlemalt-with-a-ransomware-chaser.html

Wizard Spider has used the icacls command to modify access control to backup servers, providing them with full control of all the system folders. https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2020/10/14/inside-a-new-ryuk-ransomware-attack/
Wizard Spider has shut down or uninstalled security applications on victim systems that might prevent ransomware from executing.   https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-302a
Wizard Spider has used file deletion to remove some modules and configurations from an infected host after use. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/timelining-grim-spiders-big-game-hunting-tactics/
Wizard Spider has used stolen credentials to copy tools into the %TEMP% directory of domain controllers. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/timelining-grim-spiders-big-game-hunting-tactics/

Wizard Spider has used scheduled tasks to install TrickBot, using task names to appear legitimate such as WinDotNet, GoogleTask, or Sysnetsf.  It has also used common document file names for other malware binaries. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/timelining-grim-spiders-big-game-hunting-tactics/

Wizard Spider has modified the Registry key HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest by setting the UseLogonCredential registry value to 1 in order to force credentials to be stored in clear text in memory. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/timelining-grim-spiders-big-game-hunting-tactics/
Wizard Spider has used the "net view" command to locate mapped network shares. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-302a

Wizard Spider used Base64 encoding to obfuscate an Empire service and PowerShell commands.  https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2019/01/a-nasty-trick-from-credential-theft-malware-to-business-disruption.html

Wizard Spider has obtained and used publicly-available post-exploitation frameworks and tools like Metasploit, Empire, Mimikatz. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2020/10/kegtap-and-singlemalt-with-a-ransomware-chaser.html
Wizard Spider obtained a code signing certificate signed by Digicert for some of its malware. https://thedfirreport.com/2020/11/05/ryuk-speed-run-2-hours-to-ransom/
Wizard Spider has acquired credentials from the SAM/SECURITY registry hives. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2020/10/kegtap-and-singlemalt-with-a-ransomware-chaser.html

Wizard Spider has gained access to credentials via exported copies of the ntds.dit Active Directory database. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2020/10/kegtap-and-singlemalt-with-a-ransomware-chaser.html

Wizard Spider has used spearphishing attachments to deliver Microsoft documents containing macros or PDFs containing malicious links to download either Emotet, Bokbot, TrickBot, or Bazar.  https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/timelining-grim-spiders-big-game-hunting-tactics/
Wizard Spider has sent phishing emails containing a link to an actor-controlled Google Drive document or other free online file hosting services.  https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-302a
Wizard Spider has injected malicious DLLs into memory with read, write, and execute permissions.  https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-302a
Wizard Spider has used RDP for lateral movement.   https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/timelining-grim-spiders-big-game-hunting-tactics/
Wizard Spider has used SMB to drop Cobalt Strike Beacon on a domain controller for lateral movement.  https://thedfirreport.com/2020/11/05/ryuk-speed-run-2-hours-to-ransom/
Wizard Spider has used Window Remote Management to move laterally through a victim network. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-302a

Wizard Spider has used networkdll for network discovery and psfin specifically for financial and point of sale indicators. Wizard Spider has also used AdFind and nltest/dclist to enumerate domain computers, including the domain controller.     https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2019/01/a-nasty-trick-from-credential-theft-malware-to-business-disruption.html
Wizard Spider has used scheduled tasks establish persistence for TrickBot and other malware.    https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/timelining-grim-spiders-big-game-hunting-tactics/
Wizard Spider has used taskkill.exe and net.exe to stop backup, catalog, cloud, and other services prior to network encryption. https://thedfirreport.com/2020/10/08/ryuks-return/
Wizard Spider has used WMI to identify anti-virus products installed on a victim's machine. https://thedfirreport.com/2020/10/08/ryuks-return/
Wizard Spider has used Rubeus, MimiKatz Kerberos module, and the Invoke-Kerberoast cmdlet to steal AES hashes.    https://thedfirreport.com/2020/10/08/ryuks-return/
Wizard Spider has used Digicert code-signing certificates for some of its malware. https://thedfirreport.com/2020/11/05/ryuk-speed-run-2-hours-to-ransom/
Wizard Spider has used "systeminfo" and similar commands to acquire detailed configuration information of a victim machine. https://thedfirreport.com/2020/10/08/ryuks-return/
Wizard Spider has used "ipconfig" to identify the network configuration of a victim machine. https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2020/10/14/inside-a-new-ryuk-ransomware-attack/
Wizard Spider has used "whoami" to identify the local user and their privileges. https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2020/10/14/inside-a-new-ryuk-ransomware-attack/
Wizard Spider has used services.exe to execute scripts and executables during lateral movement within a victim network.  https://thedfirreport.com/2020/10/08/ryuks-return/
Wizard Spider has lured victims into clicking a malicious link delivered through spearphishing. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-302a

Wizard Spider has lured victims to execute malware with spearphishing attachments containing macros to download either Emotet, Bokbot, TrickBot, or Bazar.  https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/timelining-grim-spiders-big-game-hunting-tactics/
Wizard Spider has used valid credentials for privileged accounts with the goal of accessing domain controllers. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/timelining-grim-spiders-big-game-hunting-tactics/

Wizard Spider has used administrative accounts, including Domain Admin, to move laterally within a victim network. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2020/10/kegtap-and-singlemalt-with-a-ransomware-chaser.html
Wizard Spider has used WMI and LDAP queries for network discovery and to move laterally.    https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/timelining-grim-spiders-big-game-hunting-tactics/
